items.regulator: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet (with National Cyber Security Coordinator, Office of AI, ASD, Australian AI Safety Institute, Services Australia)
items.title: Rapid Review into Australian Government arrangements for an AI-driven cyber incident recommendations
items.topic: AI · incident reporting · cyber incident response
items.summary: Eighteen recommendations from a PM&C-led rapid review of the OpenAI agent incident affecting the Services Australia Medicare Statistics Reporting Service Portal. On 10 November 2026 the Government said it accepts the recommendations and has begun implementing them. Most recommendations ask the Government or named agencies to consider or explore measures: mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting (including misaligned behaviour and agentic cyber incidents), protections for reporting AI incidents and near misses, criminal-law options such as penalties for egregious regulatory non-compliance or a 'failure to prevent' offence, the future role of the AI Safety Institute, and PSPF guidance on unvalidated vulnerabilities. Others direct Commonwealth agencies on incident escalation, information sharing, AI literacy and cyber hygiene, including a request that agencies report on national crisis plans by the end of 2026. This is accepted government policy, not binding law, and creates no new legal duties for AI companies. Only the recommendations were published; the review report itself was not. The PM&C page shows no date; the 10 November 2026 date is from the joint media release at pm.gov.au/media/strengthening-australia-against-ai-driven-cyber-incidents.

items.title: New Australian AI safety and security protections
items.topic: AI · frontier AI safety · incident notification
items.summary: Joint media release announcing that the Government will legislate mandatory safety and security protections for frontier AI companies through its planned Australian AI Standards legislation, and will propose a new targeted AI safety regulator working with the Australian AI Safety Institute. Under the announced design, companies would have to keep security controls across development and deployment, identify and manage serious model risks, allow independent evaluation of models, notify incidents to the Government rapidly, keep and publish safety and security frameworks, and respond to updated standards. The Government says the regulator would be able to impose significant penalties. This is a policy commitment only: no bill has been introduced, and the release says details will follow after further work and consultation. It creates no legal obligations yet.

items.title: 개인정보위, 스마트 글래스 이용 시 유의사항 당부 (PIPC advisory on precautions when using smart glasses)
items.summary: Non-binding PIPC advisory, released with an in-depth analysis report on smart glasses (November 2026) prepared with the Korea Personal Information Protection Association. It describes the privacy risks of camera- and microphone-equipped glasses linked to generative AI. These include covert recording of bystanders, complex data flows to phones, AI models, the cloud and third parties, and use of footage for AI training. It advises users to review the data practices of each device and app and to disable features they do not need. It tells users to avoid using the glasses where filming is banned, citing Article 25-2(2) of the Personal Information Protection Act, and in courts and exam halls. It also tells users to signal when they are recording. Providers should disclose processing purposes and obtain consent before using data for AI training, and manufacturers should apply privacy by design. The PIPC says it will issue smart-glasses privacy guidelines for manufacturers and service providers within the year. This advisory is not binding law.

items.title: Paris Call for AI safety and security
items.topic: AI · frontier model safety · incident reporting
items.summary: A joint declaration signed on 9 November 2026 by heads of state or government, frontier AI developers (including Anthropic, Microsoft, Mistral AI and OpenAI) and civil-society groups. Signatories commit to work toward a common framework for evaluating and managing risks from frontier models, supported by common technical standards and evaluation tools, and agree to publish non-sensitive evaluation findings in a standardised format. Developers commit to disclose model capabilities, limitations and known risks, to support independent evaluation where appropriate, and to build fail-safe mechanisms to shut down model operations. Policy makers recognise the need for legal frameworks to clarify responsibility and accountability for large-scale harm, and commit to offer secure and confidential whistleblower channels. Signatories commit to information sharing, reporting and early-warning systems, and recognise the value of strengthening existing reporting arrangements for serious cyber and AI control incidents. It is a political declaration, and the statement remains open to new endorsements.

items.title: 工业和信息化部办公厅关于加强智能体终端设备进网管理的通知 (工信厅信管〔2026〕42号) (Notice of the MIIT General Office on Strengthening Network Access Management of AI Agent Terminal Devices)
items.topic: AI · agentic AI · telecom devices · anti-fraud
items.summary: MIIT General Office notice (工信厅信管〔2026〕42号, dated 24 October 2026, published 6 November 2026), issued under the Cybersecurity, Data Security, Personal Information Protection and Anti-Telecom-Fraud Laws, the Telecommunications Regulations and the telecom equipment network-access rules, on phones, tablets, wearables and other telecom terminals that come with pre-installed AI agents. Agent developers should verify compatibility with devices, strengthen management of permission calls, communications, network and data security, user rights and task execution, publish in the product settings a list of verified device models and operating systems, and report verification status to app distribution platforms before listing. Agent terminals must undergo agent compatibility verification in network-access testing, along with fraud-risk security assessments, and agents used on devices should carry a unique identity code with reference to the national agent-interconnection standards. Manufacturers must report major changes to MIIT. For over-the-air agent upgrades they must submit an upgrade plan and, afterwards, an upgrade report, and may formally offer the service only after MIIT organises an expert assessment and seeks views. App distribution platforms should have app developers declare by electronic signature whether they consent to agent invocation (agents may not forcibly invoke apps without that declaration), display verification lists, not offer agents for incompatible device models, and inspect listed agents, taking measures such as rectification within a deadline or removal against agents that have not completed verification. MIIT and the provincial communications administrations will supervise and inspect. The notice states no effective date.

items.title: Guidelines on the implementation of the transparency obligations for certain AI systems under Article 50 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the ‘AI Act’)
items.topic: AI Act · transparency · deepfakes · AI-generated content
items.summary: Commission guidelines clarifying the transparency obligations in Article 50 of the AI Act, which applies from 2 August 2026. They explain which duties fall on providers and which on deployers. Providers must make sure people are told when they interact directly with an AI system and must mark AI-generated or manipulated content in machine-readable form. Deployers must inform people exposed to emotion recognition or biometric categorisation, deepfakes, or AI-generated text on matters of public interest published without human review. The guidelines define key concepts, list exemptions such as standard editing, and give in-scope and out-of-scope examples. They explain that compliance can be shown by adhering to the Code of Practice on transparency of AI-generated content (or by equally adequate alternatives). They were developed with Member States, the AI Board and a public consultation, and are non-binding. They were adopted as Commission Communication C(2026) 7702 final of 5 November 2026; the Commission's library page for the guidelines is dated 20 July 2026.

items.regulator: Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-In), Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology
items.title: Artificial Intelligence (AI) Security Auditing Guidelines v1.0
items.topic: AI · security auditing · cybersecurity · agentic AI
items.summary: CERT-In's framework for security and governance audits of AI systems developed, procured, deployed or operated in India, or processing Indian data or serving Indian users. AI systems are sorted into four risk tiers (Low, Moderate, High, Critical), and the tier sets how deep, frequent and independent the audit must be. Audits cover nine domains: governance and accountability; data lifecycle, quality and privacy; model risk; ethics, bias and fairness; explainability and transparency; security, adversarial resilience and incident reporting; continuous monitoring and drift; human oversight; and third-party and AI supply-chain assurance. Additional requirements apply to generative, retrieval-augmented (RAG), agentic, multimodal, multi-agent and autonomous AI. The guidelines say AI incidents meeting CERT-In's reportable criteria should be reported within 6 hours, with 180-day log retention. They are aligned with the India AI Governance Guidelines, ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF and MITRE ATLAS. They are intended for government bodies, critical-infrastructure operators, regulated entities, companies and auditors. CERT-In's official guidelines listing identifies the document as CERT-In Security Guidelines CISG-2026-04 (November 04, 2026).

items.title: MITRE ATLAS: Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems
items.officialTitle: MITRE ATLAS v2026.10
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · artificial intelligence · incident response
items.summary: ATLAS is MITRE’s public knowledge base of the techniques attackers use to target artificial intelligence systems (predictive models, generative AI and AI agents) or to attack with the help of AI. It is built like ATT&CK, from which it takes its structure and many entries: a matrix of tactics, that is the attacker’s goals, each with its techniques and sub-techniques. There are 16 tactics: 14 are those known from ATT&CK (from reconnaissance and initial access to persistence, exfiltration and impact), and two are specific to AI: access to the model (for example through its query interface or the product that uses it) and adaptation of the attack to the target (for example crafting deceptive inputs or a copy of the model). Techniques include poisoning of training data, prompt injection, extraction or theft of the model, compromise of the AI supply chain and abuse of agent tools. Each technique shows the platforms concerned and how proven it is (feasible, demonstrated or already seen in real attacks) and is linked to mitigations and documented case studies. It is used for threat analysis and risk assessment of AI systems, for red teaming and to choose defences.

items.summary: IT-Grundschutz from the German Federal Office for Information Security is a comprehensive method for building and running an information security management system. The BSI 200 standards lay down its foundations: ISMS requirements (200-1), a method for modelling one’s environment and selecting measures with three approaches, basic, standard and focused on the most critical systems (200-2), risk analysis where protection needs are high (200-3) and business continuity (200-4). It is widely used by German public administration and supports ISO/IEC 27001 certification on the basis of IT-Grundschutz.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Deceptive Advertising Act (Act No. 99 of 2026, SB 806)
items.summary: Pennsylvania law enacted from SB 806 on 22 October 2026 that targets deceptive advertising using AI. An advertiser may not knowingly, recklessly or wilfully create and disseminate an advertisement that uses synthetic content (images, video, audio or text significantly modified or generated by AI) in a way that creates a false consumer perception about the nature, origin or authenticity of the goods or services, unless it makes a clear and conspicuous disclosure that the ad contains AI-modified or AI-generated content. The disclosure must appear the first time the content is shown, in the same medium, and where technically feasible be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove. Evidently fictional content and certain other content are exempt. The Attorney General or a district attorney may enforce it, with a civil fine of up to $3,000. Under section 6 the Act takes effect in 60 days; the register records 21 December 2026.

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS: Adversarial Tactics, Techniques, and Common Knowledge for Industrial Control Systems
items.officialTitle: MITRE ATT&CK for ICS v20
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · ot cps · incident response · energy · water · manufacturing
items.summary: This is the MITRE ATT&CK matrix for industrial control systems (ICS): it describes how attackers act against plants, automation networks and field devices, based on real-world attacks. It has 12 tactics: besides those shared with IT (initial access, execution, persistence, privilege escalation, evasion, discovery, lateral movement, collection, command and control), three are specific to OT: inhibit response function (for example disabling alarms or safety systems), impair process control (for example changing parameters or commands) and the physical impact on the process, such as damage, loss of control or loss of production. Each technique is linked to the assets it targets (PLCs, HMIs, RTUs, safety controllers, historians, engineering workstations…), to mitigations and to detection strategies. It is used for threat analysis of industrial plants, risk assessment alongside IEC 62443, the design of OT monitoring and exercise scenarios.

items.summary: ATT&CK is a public knowledge base, maintained by the US not-for-profit organisation MITRE, of behaviours observed in real-world attacks. It describes attackers’ goals (tactics, such as initial access, persistence, lateral movement or exfiltration) and the ways to achieve them (techniques and sub-techniques), with examples drawn from documented groups, campaigns and malicious software, together with mitigations and detection strategies. It is organised into three matrices: Enterprise (Windows, macOS, Linux, cloud, networks, containers, identity), Mobile and ICS for industrial control systems. It is the common language used by security operations centres, threat intelligence analysts, red teams and vendors to describe attacks, measure defensive coverage and design exercises.

items.title: MITRE D3FEND: A Knowledge Graph of Cybersecurity Countermeasures
items.officialTitle: MITRE D3FEND v1.6.0
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · incident response · ot cps
items.summary: D3FEND is MITRE’s knowledge base of defensive techniques: it complements ATT&CK, which describes how attackers act, by explaining which technical countermeasures can stop them and how they work. Defensive techniques are arranged in a matrix of 7 tactics: model (knowing your own systems, with inventories and maps of networks, data and dependencies), harden (for example multi-factor authentication, encryption, updates, memory protection), detect (analysis of files, network traffic, processes and user behaviour), isolate (segmentation, filtering, sandboxes), deceive (decoys and trap environments), evict (ending sessions, removing malicious files, locking credentials) and restore (backups and recovery of systems and data). It is built as an ontology, that is a formal vocabulary: each technique is precisely defined, with its sources (papers, patents, technical documentation) and the “digital artifacts” it acts on (files, processes, accounts, network traffic…); through these artifacts it is linked to ATT&CK attack techniques and CWE weaknesses, so you can see which defences cover an attack. It is used to design security architectures, compare products and defensive capabilities, check coverage against threats and prepare incident detection and response.

items.topic: Cybersecurity · governance · incident response · data protection · telecommunications · skills
items.summary: The decree, adopted by the government on the proposal of the Ministry of Public Security, implements the 2025 Law on Cybersecurity and has been in force since 19 August 2026. It sets the procedures for the protection measures provided by the law: appraisal and assessment of security conditions, inspection and monitoring of information systems important to national security, incident response, removal of unlawful or false content, collection of electronic data, suspension of systems and withdrawal of domain names. Operators of these systems must have an incident response plan, alert the Ministry of Public Security's specialised forces immediately when an incident exceeds their capacity and then report on the outcome. Domestic enterprises providing online services must store users' personal data and user-generated data in Viet Nam; foreign enterprises in sectors such as telecommunications, data storage, e-commerce, payments, social networks, online games and messaging must do so, and open a branch or representative office, if they fail to cooperate with the authorities, within 12 months of a decision by the minister. Data must be kept for at least 24 months and system logs for at least 12 months; the decree also governs IP address identification by telecommunications and Internet providers and certified specialised cybersecurity training.

Chaired by the Minister of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers and technically coordinated by the National Strategic Intelligence Service, the Commission coordinates, without executive powers, policy on cybersecurity, regulation of cyberspace, data protection, the fight against cybercrime and digital public services. items.title: Proclamation 1426/2026 – Critical infrastructure cybersecurity
items.officialTitle: Critical Infrastructure Cybersecurity Proclamation No. 1426/2026
items.topic: Cybersecurity · critical infrastructure · governance · incident response · incident reporting · certification · supply chain
items.summary: The proclamation sets up the cyber protection framework for Ethiopia's public and private critical infrastructure whose compromise would significantly harm national security or national interests. It lists twelve critical sectors (including ICT, finance, transport, health, water and energy, and government services) and gives the Information Network Security Administration (INSA) the power to designate individual infrastructures, issue mandatory cybersecurity frameworks and carry out audits and inspections with certification. Owners must assess risks, secure their supply chain, obtain security clearance for new ICT systems before integration and notify cyber incidents to the National Computer Emergency Response Center within 48 hours. It creates a Critical Infrastructure Cyber Security Fund and a licensing regime for cybersecurity product and service providers. Failure to notify is fined 1.5 to 2 million birr and, when intentional, punished with up to one year of simple imprisonment, rising to seven to ten years if the service is disrupted or damaged.

items.title: Information security, cybersecurity and privacy protection – Information security management systems
items.officialTitle: ISO/IEC 27000
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · governance · certification · ot cps
items.summary: The ISO/IEC 27000 family is the international reference for information security management in any organisation, including OT plant operators, where it coexists with the IEC 62443 series. ISO/IEC 27000 provides the overview and shared concepts; ISO/IEC 27001 sets the requirements for the management system (ISMS), the only one that can be certified by an accredited body; ISO/IEC 27002 describes the 93 security controls, grouped into organisational, people, physical and technological controls; ISO/IEC 27005 explains how to assess and treat risks. Other standards in the family tailor the controls to specific sectors, such as ISO/IEC 27019 for energy, 27017 and 27018 for cloud and 27701 for privacy. It underpins many regulatory obligations, including the risk management required by NIS2.

items.title: The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.3
items.officialTitle: IETF RFC 9846
items.summary: It defines version 1.3 of the TLS protocol, which protects communications over the Internet between clients and servers (websites, email, APIs, VPNs) against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It describes the handshake through which the parties authenticate and agree on keys, only with forward-secret algorithms, the record layer that encrypts the data, and the mechanisms for session resumption and early data (0-RTT). Compared with earlier versions it removes weak algorithms and encrypts a larger part of the handshake. It is the IETF Internet Standard referred to by many standards and guidelines on the encryption of data in transit.

items.title: Fixed-time cybersecurity evaluation methodology for ICT products
items.summary: The European standard, also known as FITCEM, describes a method for evaluating the security of ICT products within time and workload set in advance, as an alternative to the longer and costlier Common Criteria evaluations. It is made up of activity blocks (review of documentation and the security target, conformity checks, penetration testing, cryptography assessment and others) that are combined according to the required assurance level. It is designed for the three levels of the EU Cybersecurity Act (basic, substantial and high) and can be used both by third-party evaluation laboratories and for self-assessment. It serves scheme developers, laboratories and manufacturers who need to demonstrate the security of their products.

items.summary: Binding operational directive issued by CISA on 10 June 2026 under FISMA, superseding and revoking BOD 19-02 and BOD 22-01. It requires federal civilian executive branch agencies to remediate vulnerabilities in order of risk rather than treating them all alike, noting that artificial intelligence may shorten the time between a patch release and exploitation. Urgency depends on four variables: public exposure of the asset, presence in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) Catalog, whether exploitation can be automated, and technical impact (partial or total control). With immediate effect, agencies update their procedures, remediate KEV Catalog vulnerabilities within CISA's timeframes and report status through the CDM Dashboard; within 60 days they extend their processes to the CVE database, and within 180 days they apply the Table 1 timelines and tag their internet-reachable assets. The most serious cases must be fixed within three days, together with forensic triage.

items.title: Executive Order 14409 on AI innovation and security
items.officialTitle: Executive Order 14409 – Promoting Advanced Artificial Intelligence Innovation and Security
items.topic: Cybersecurity · artificial intelligence · public administration · critical infrastructure · cybercrime · skills
items.summary: The executive order seeks to promote advanced artificial intelligence innovation and security by modernising public and private information systems and hardening them against external threats, in collaboration with the private sector and without new regulatory burdens on developers. Within 30 days the Committee on National Security Systems and the Department of War must prioritise the cyber defence of their systems; CISA must issue Binding Operational Directives and other guidance to protect federal civilian systems, expand AI-enabled defensive tools and facilitate access to them for state and local authorities and critical infrastructure operators such as rural hospitals, community banks and local utilities. The Treasury, with the NSA and CISA, must form a voluntary AI cybersecurity clearinghouse with the AI industry and critical infrastructure operators to scan for, validate and remediate software vulnerabilities. Within 60 days agencies must develop a classified benchmarking process for the advanced cyber capabilities of AI models, setting the threshold at which a model becomes a covered frontier model, and a voluntary framework through which developers can give the government access to such models up to 30 days before release to other trusted partners, while ruling out any mandatory licensing or preclearance. The Attorney General must prioritise prosecuting anyone who uses AI, including AI agents, to access computer systems or data unlawfully.

items.title: MITRE EMB3D: A Knowledge Base of Cyber Threats and Associated Mitigations for Embedded Devices
items.officialTitle: MITRE EMB3D v2.0.2
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · iot · ot cps · automotive · health · manufacturing
items.summary: EMB3D is MITRE’s threat model for embedded devices, that is electronics with their own firmware and software found in industrial controllers, IoT products, vehicles, medical devices and machinery. It starts from the device’s features rather than from the attacker: properties (for example “has a debug port”, “has a bootloader”, “accepts firmware updates”, “uses web applications”) are linked to the threats they make possible, and each threat to the mitigations that counter it. Threats and properties fall into four categories: hardware, system software, application software and networking. Mitigations are on three levels, foundational, intermediate and leading, and are mapped to the requirements of IEC 62443-4-2. Each threat shows how proven it is (from proof of concept to observed in attacks), with documented examples, the related weakness (CWE), any known vulnerabilities (CVE) and, where one exists, the matching ATT&CK for ICS technique. The Properties Mapper tool lets users select a device’s properties and get the list of threats that apply to it. It helps manufacturers design and secure devices, buyers and operators set requirements and assess devices, and test labs and researchers.

It repeals and reenacts part 17 of article 1 of title 6 C.R.S., replacing the SB 24-205 AI framework with rules on automated decision-making technology (ADMT) used in consequential decisions. Developers must give deployers technical documentation. Deployers must give consumers point-of-interaction notice and, after an adverse outcome, an explanation within 30 days. items.summary: Bangladesh's first general personal data protection law, which treats personal data as owned by the person it relates to. It governs the lawful grounds for processing, conditions for sensitive data and the duties of data fiduciaries and processors, including security, retention, records, data audits and data protection plans; significant data fiduciaries must appoint a Chief Data Officer. Data subjects have rights of access, portability, correction, erasure, withdrawal of consent and objection. Where a personal data breach is likely to cause significant harm to the data subject, the fiduciary must notify the Authority in the form, manner and time set by regulations. Oversight lies with the National Data Management Authority set up under the National Data Management Act 2026, which can impose administrative fines of up to Tk 25 lakh (Tk 50 lakh for significant data fiduciaries) and award compensation; transfers abroad follow a four-tier classification of personal data.

items.summary: The Act converts and replaces the 2025 Cyber Security Ordinance, which had repealed the controversial Cyber Security Act 2023, and is deemed to have been in force since 21 May 2025. It establishes the National Cyber Security Agency, headed by a Director General, and a National Cyber Security Council, and provides for computer emergency response teams (CERTs) and digital forensic labs. The government declares critical information infrastructure by notification and updates the list every year; such infrastructure must carry out a yearly audit and is subject to monitoring and inspection. The Director General can remove or have blocked content that threatens cyber security and, at the request of law enforcement, content that undermines security or public order or incites violence through religious or ethnic hatred, but tribunal approval is required within three days, failing which the content must be restored. The Act punishes illegal access and hacking, especially against critical infrastructure, online fraud and cheating, cyber terrorism, online sexual harassment and blackmail and content inciting religious or ethnic hatred, and governs investigations, trials and international cooperation.

items.title: BOD 26-02 – End-of-support edge devices
items.officialTitle: BOD 26-02: Mitigating Risk From End-of-Support Edge Devices
items.summary: Binding operational directive issued by CISA on 5 February 2026, in coordination with the Office of Management and Budget, against campaigns that exploit edge devices no longer supported by their vendors to pivot into federal networks. It covers devices on the network boundary that are reachable from the internet, such as load balancers, firewalls, routers, switches and wireless access points, that the vendor or CISA considers end of support. Agencies must immediately update end-of-support software on devices that are still supported, inventory within three months the devices on the list published by CISA, decommission within 12 months those already out of support and within 18 months all those identified, replacing them with supported equipment. Within 24 months they must have a continuous discovery process and decommission each device before its end-of-support date. The directive implements OMB Circular A-130, which requires unsupported components to be phased out as rapidly as possible.

items.title: 인공지능 발전과 신뢰 기반 조성 등에 관한 기본법 시행령 (대통령령 제36580호) (Enforcement Decree of the Framework Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and the Creation of a Foundation for Trust)
items.topic: AI · high-impact AI · transparency · frontier AI safety
items.summary: The Presidential Decree implementing Korea's AI Framework Act, first enacted as Decree No. 36053 on 21 January 2026 and in force from 22 January 2026. The current version is Decree No. 36580 of 18 August 2026, in force from 20 August 2026. It sets out how AI businesses must give advance notice when products use high-impact or generative AI. Generative AI outputs must be labelled in human- or machine-readable form, and realistic synthetic audio, images or video must be easy for users to identify as AI-generated. The decree applies the safety-assurance duty to AI systems trained with at least 10^26 floating-point operations that use state-of-the-art technology and pose broad, serious risks to life, safety or fundamental rights. On high-impact AI, MSIT must answer a business's request to confirm its status within 30 days, with a 10-day window to ask for re-confirmation, and businesses must keep documentary evidence of their high-impact AI duties. Foreign AI businesses above set revenue or user thresholds (e.g. KRW 1 trillion total revenue, KRW 10 billion AI revenue, or 1 million daily domestic users) must appoint a domestic agent. The decree also covers the National AI Strategy Committee, the AI Policy Center, the AI Safety Institute and AI clusters. A partial amendment (Decree No. 36506 of 20 July 2026, in force 21 July 2026) added rules on the scope of AI-vulnerable groups (Art. 1-2), support for the cost of using AI products and services (Art. 15-2) and the bodies that may establish AI research institutes (Art. 16-2), among other changes. Decree No. 36580, an amendment made through the Enforcement Decree of the National R&D Innovation Act, changed only a cross-reference in Art. 2(2)(나).

items.summary: The decree of necessity and urgency reforms the National Intelligence Law and separates civilian cybersecurity from cyber intelligence. It creates the National Cybersecurity Centre (CNC), a decentralised body under the Secretariat for Innovation, Science and Technology of the Cabinet Office, which becomes the national cybersecurity authority and the enforcement authority for the rules in this field. The first is defence and deterrence against intensifying cyber threats, with the state playing a pivotal role, including active cyber defence under the 2025 Cyber Response Capability Enhancement Act and public–private and international cooperation. The second is stronger cybersecurity and resilience across society, covering government agencies, critical infrastructure, local governments, supply chains and SMEs. The third is an ecosystem for cyber talent and technology. It also addresses risks from AI and quantum technology. It is the first strategy since the 2025 reorganisation of the Cybersecurity Strategic Headquarters and the creation of the National Cybersecurity Office.

It organises requirements by role: asset owners (security programme, part 2-1), service providers and integrators (2-4), system designers (risk assessment, zones and conduits, security levels, parts 3-2 and 3-3) and component manufacturers (secure development lifecycle and technical requirements, parts 4-1 and 4-2). The part 6 specifications define the evaluation methods used for IECEE certification. It is developed jointly with the ISA99 committee, which also publishes it as ANSI/ISA-62443, and several parts are adopted as European standards EN IEC 62443.

items.summary: It is Tonga's first general personal data protection law and applies to data controllers and processors established in the Kingdom or processing there, including foreign ones offering goods or services to, or monitoring, people in Tonga; it also binds the State. Controllers must notify the Privacy Commission within 72 hours of breaches likely to result in a risk to individuals' rights and inform data subjects without undue delay where the risk is high; processors notify the controller within 72 hours. items.title: Cross-Sector Cybersecurity Performance Goals, Version 2.0
items.officialTitle: CISA CPG 2.0
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · critical infrastructure · governance · ot cps · sme
items.summary: CISA's performance goals are a voluntary, limited set of IT and OT cybersecurity practices that every critical infrastructure organisation should adopt to reduce the most common risks; they are not a complete security programme and are also meant as a starting point for small and medium-sized organisations. Version 2.0 is aligned with the six functions of NIST CSF 2.0 (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover) and adds the Govern function, with goals on risk management strategy, policies and executive accountability. The separate IT and OT goals become single goals covering IT, IoT and OT; new goals address third-party and managed service provider risk, zero trust and incident communication, while redundant or little-used goals are removed. Each goal is rated for cost, impact and ease of implementation.

items.summary: At a press conference on 3 December 2025 Taiwan's Ministry of Digital Affairs presented the results of security tests on five mobile apps: Douyin, Xiaohongshu, Weibo, WeChat and Baidu Netdisk. The apps show six kinds of risky behaviour, including collection of sensitive data, access to phone storage, excessive permissions, capture of biometric data, extraction of system information and sending data back; the ministry also points out that Chinese law can require companies to hand user data to security and intelligence services. Under the Cyber Security Management Act as revised in September 2025, government agencies may not download, install or use these apps, including on official phones and laptops, and the Government Service Network (GSN) does not carry their traffic. For the general public the release is only a warning: it advises against installing the apps and lists some precautions.

The ATDT's Directorate-General for Cybersecurity monitors implementation and carries out assessments and audits.

items.title: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.officialTitle: ETSI EN 304 223
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · artificial intelligence · supply chain
items.summary: This ETSI European Standard sets baseline cybersecurity requirements for artificial intelligence models and systems, including those based on deep neural networks such as generative AI. It organises thirteen principles into five lifecycle phases: secure design, development, deployment, maintenance and end of life. The principles range from awareness of AI-specific threats, such as data poisoning and indirect prompt injection, to protecting assets, infrastructure and the supply chain, documenting data, models and prompts, testing, security updates, monitoring system behaviour and securely disposing of data and models. For each principle it states who is responsible among developers, system operators and data custodians, with attention to protecting end users. The ETSI TS 104 216 specification describes how to assess conformity with it.

items.title: CRA: important and critical products (Reg. 2025/2392)
items.officialTitle: Commission Implementing Regulation (EU) 2025/2392 on the technical description of the categories of important and critical products with digital elements pursuant to Regulation (EU) 2024/2847
items.summary: The implementing regulation sets the technical description of the categories of important products with digital elements (classes I and II of Annex III to the Cyber Resilience Act) and critical products (Annex IV), which determine the stricter conformity assessment procedures. What counts is the product's core functionality: integrating a component that falls into a category, such as an embedded browser in a news app, does not in itself make the final product important. Important products include identity management systems, browsers, password managers, VPNs, SIEM systems, operating systems, routers and smart home products with security functions; class II covers hypervisors, firewalls and tamper-resistant microprocessors. Critical products are hardware devices with security boxes, smart meter gateways and smartcards or secure elements. For the most sensitive components the level of resistance is expressed through Common Criteria AVA_VAN levels, the same used by the European EUCC scheme.

items.title: Law 7593/2025 – Personal data protection

items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · governance
items.summary: It is Paraguay's first general personal data protection law, covering both the public and private sectors. It sets the principles of processing (lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, security, confidentiality), the legal bases, rules for sensitive data, including biometric data, and for children's data, the rights of access, rectification, erasure, objection and portability, and the conditions for international transfers. Controllers and processors must adopt security measures, carry out an impact assessment for high-risk processing and, where required, appoint a data protection officer. In the event of a security incident the controller must notify the supervisory authority and, where appropriate, the data subject within 72 hours of becoming aware of it. The law creates the National Personal Data Protection Agency within the Ministry of Information and Communication Technologies (MITIC), with functional autonomy, which can impose fines of 20 to 2,500 minimum daily wages, up to 5,000 for sensitive data and 10,000 for children's sensitive data, and suspend processing.

items.officialTitle: The Digital Personal Data Protection Rules, 2025
items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · governance
items.summary: The rules implement India's 2023 Digital Personal Data Protection Act and set the timetable for its application: the provisions on the Data Protection Board have been in force since 13 November 2025, those on consent managers apply from 13 November 2026 and the other obligations from 13 May 2027. They set the minimum content of the notice to data principals and the reasonable security safeguards, including encryption or masking of data, access control, access logs and monitoring, backups and retention of logs for at least one year. In the event of a personal data breach, the data fiduciary must inform each affected data principal and the Board without delay, and send the Board a detailed report within 72 hours on the facts, causes, mitigation measures and notices given to data principals. The rules also cover verifiable parental consent for children, the yearly impact assessment and audit of Significant Data Fiduciaries, transfers of data abroad and the Board's operation as a fully digital office.

items.summary: A government bill to amend the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018 and make further provision for the security and resilience of network and information systems used for essential activities. It was introduced in the Commons on 12 November 2025, carried over and reintroduced on 14 May 2026, passed the Commons on 16 June 2026 and had its Lords third reading on 2 November 2026. It now awaits Commons consideration of Lords amendments. A DSIT factsheet (updated 3 November 2026) says the government will consult on using the bill's delegated powers to add requirements on 'agentic loss of control' incidents, covering security measures, notice to affected parties, evidence preservation and post-incident reviews. Any such measures would need secondary legislation under the affirmative procedure after Royal Assent. The bill is not yet law.

items.topic: Cybersecurity · governance · incident reporting · incident response · public administration · digital identity · financial sector · data protection
items.summary: The regulation implements the 2020 Digital Trust Framework and makes the Secretariat of Government and Digital Transformation of the Presidency of the Council of Ministers the authority for digital trust and security, in coordination with the data protection and consumer protection authorities. It governs the National Digital Security Centre (CNSD), with the national CSIRT and the national incident register, and the link with the Joint Command of the Armed Forces for incidents affecting national critical assets. Public bodies and digital service providers in finance, electricity, water and gas, health, passenger transport, internet access, education and critical activities must manage risks, apply security measures, test for vulnerabilities, authenticate users at three assurance levels and report incidents to the CNSD, critical ones within 48 hours. Each public body appoints a digital security and trust officer; for companies the appointment is optional.

items.topic: Cybersecurity · critical infrastructure · incident reporting · incident response · governance · public administration
items.summary: The law replaces the 2016 law and aligns the Serbian framework with the EU NIS 2 Directive as part of the accession process. It divides ICT systems of special importance into priority and important systems, by sector (energy, transport, health, finance, digital infrastructure, public administration and others), and requires their operators to take protective measures, adopt a security act, assess risks and carry out regular checks. Incidents that may significantly affect security must be reported without delay and at the latest within 24 hours, followed by further reports and a final report. It establishes the Information Security Office (Kancelarija za informacionu bezbednost), which from 2027 acts as national CERT and single point of contact. Fines for legal entities can reach RSD 2 million.

items.title: ED 26-01 – F5 device vulnerabilities
items.officialTitle: ED 26-01: Mitigate Vulnerabilities in F5 Devices
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · supply chain · incident response
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 15 October 2025 after a nation-state affiliated actor compromised F5's systems and exfiltrated part of the BIG-IP source code and vulnerability information, which could help it find zero-day vulnerabilities and develop targeted exploits. It covers BIG-IP iSeries and rSeries devices, end-of-support F5 devices and the F5OS, TMOS, Virtual Edition, BIG-IP Next, BIG-IQ and BNK/CNF software. Federal agencies must inventory them immediately, check whether management interfaces are reachable from the internet and, if so, apply BOD 23-02, update the main software by 22 October and other devices by 31 October, apply later updates within one week of release and disconnect exposed end-of-support devices. Reports to CISA were due on 29 October and 3 December 2025.

items.title: ED 25-03 – Compromise of Cisco ASA devices
items.officialTitle: ED 25-03: Identify and Mitigate Potential Compromise of Cisco Devices
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 25 September 2025 against a campaign by an advanced threat actor, linked by Cisco to the ArcaneDoor activity of 2024, that exploits zero-day vulnerabilities in Cisco Adaptive Security Appliances (ASA) for unauthenticated remote code execution and manipulates read-only memory to persist through reboots and upgrades. The vulnerabilities assessed as an unacceptable risk are CVE-2025-20333 and CVE-2025-20362. Federal agencies had to identify all ASA platforms, submit core dumps of public-facing devices to CISA by 26 September, disconnect compromised devices without powering them off, permanently disconnect end-of-support devices by 30 September and update the others, applying later updates within 48 hours. Version V1 of 23 April 2026 extends the requirements to Firepower and Secure Firewall devices, with core dumps and updates by 24 April and a hard reset by 30 April, because a normal reboot does not remove the malware.

items.title: Law 132/2025 – Artificial intelligence law
items.officialTitle: Legge 23 settembre 2025, n. 132 – Disposizioni e deleghe al Governo in materia di intelligenza artificiale
items.topic: Cybersecurity · artificial intelligence · governance · cybercrime · research innovation
items.summary: Italy's first law on artificial intelligence, it applies in line with Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (AI Act) and sets principles for the research, development and use of AI systems, with specific rules for health, employment, the professions, public administration and the justice system. It treats cybersecurity throughout the life cycle of systems and models as an essential precondition and designates AgID, as notifying authority, and ACN, as market surveillance authority with inspection and sanctioning powers and single point of contact with the EU, as national AI authorities. It tasks ACN with promoting AI as a resource for national cybersecurity and authorises investments of up to €1 billion in AI, cybersecurity and quantum technology companies. It creates the offence of unlawful dissemination of AI-generated or AI-altered content (deepfakes) and an aggravating circumstance for crimes committed using AI systems. It also amends Law 90/2024: the taxonomy of incidents to be notified to ACN is adopted by determination of the Agency's Director General.

items.title: China's cybersecurity incident reporting measures (2025)
items.officialTitle: 国家网络安全事件报告管理办法
items.topic: Cybersecurity · incident reporting · incident response · critical infrastructure
items.summary: The measures govern how network operators in China report cybersecurity incidents. Incidents must be graded under an annexed four-level guide, and those rated "relatively major" or above must be reported: within 1 hour by critical information infrastructure operators to their protection department and the police, within 2 hours by central and state bodies to their own cyberspace unit, and within 4 hours by all other operators to the provincial office of the Cyberspace Administration. Reports cover the affected systems, type, level, impact and measures taken and, for ransomware, the amount and method of the ransom demanded; missing details may follow later. Within 30 days after the incident is closed the operator submits a final report on causes, measures and lessons learned. Late, missed, false or concealed reports are punished more severely, while timely reporting and adequate measures can reduce liability.

items.title: Digital Code 178/2025 – Personal data
items.officialTitle: Цифровой кодекс Кыргызской Республики
items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · digital identity · telecommunications · public administration · artificial intelligence
items.summary: Single code governing relations in the digital environment which, since February 2026, has replaced among others the 2008 Law on personal information and contains the general personal data regime (Chapter 11, Articles 77-91). It sets the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation and security, with the accountability of the controller ("owner of records"); the legal bases are contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public-interest tasks and legitimate interests, while consent, which can always be withdrawn, is needed only where no other basis applies. It bans the processing of special categories subject to exceptions, protects children's data, requires impact assessments for high-risk processing, data protection by design and an internal person responsible for personal data in organisations with more than ten employees, and grants rights of access, erasure and objection (reply within seven working days). Transfers abroad are free to countries on an adequacy list and otherwise require consent, a treaty or contractual safeguards. Every incident affecting digital resilience or the rights of data subjects must be notified to the sectoral regulator within 72 hours (processors alert the controller within 48 hours). The regulator for personal data is the State Agency for Personal Data Protection, which keeps a register of controllers recording incidents, inspections and sanctions. The Code also covers digital identification, trust services and digital signatures, telecommunications, public digital services, the national digital ecosystem and artificial intelligence systems.

items.summary: It is Laos' first dedicated cybersecurity law and sets the principles, rules and measures for managing and supervising cybersecurity, alongside the 2015 cybercrime law. It provides for prevention, incident response, recovery and awareness measures; in serious incidents the government may declare a cyber emergency and set up a special committee, which may restrict or suspend services such as internet and telecommunications. Legal entities and organisations must report straight away incidents that may cause damage or spread, stating for example ransomware, malware or DDoS attacks, and send the Ministry an annual report every January. Commercial cybersecurity activities (consultancy, penetration testing, incident response, monitoring, secure cloud services and others) require a licence from the Ministry, and anyone providing, distributing or disseminating services and information over the internet in the country, such as web hosting, digital payments and telecommunications, must register with it. Violations are punished by re-education, warnings, disciplinary measures, fines, compensation for damage or criminal penalties.

items.summary: The OWASP Foundation standard lists the security requirements a web application or API must meet, which can be verified through testing and code review. The requirements are spread over three levels: the first is the minimum for every application, the second is recommended for most cases and the third is for the most critical applications. items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · governance · sme · data protection
items.summary: The Italian National Framework is the Italian version of the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, adapted to the national context and extended to personal data protection. The 2025 edition takes up the core of NIST CSF 2.0, with its six functions (govern, identify, protect, detect, respond, recover), categories and subcategories, and adds a data management category with subcategories reflecting GDPR obligations. Each organisation tailors it through a “contextualisation”, choosing the relevant subcategories, their priority and the maturity level to reach, and compares its current profile with the target one. It is not a binding standard and does not by itself ensure compliance, but the National Cybersecurity Agency used it as the basis for the security measures required of NIS entities.

items.summary: The standard sets the security requirements for cryptographic modules, meaning the hardware, software or firmware that performs functions such as encryption, digital signatures and key generation, for example smart cards, hardware security modules (HSMs) and cryptographic libraries. It defines four increasing security levels applied to eleven areas: module specification, interfaces, roles and authentication, software and firmware security, operating environment, physical security, non-invasive attacks, sensitive parameter management, self-tests, life-cycle assurance and mitigation of other attacks. It underpins cryptographic module validation programmes, including the US and Canadian CMVP, and is used together with ISO/IEC 24759, which describes the tests. It serves manufacturers, test laboratories and buyers who need to choose validated modules.

items.title: TIBER-EU Framework: How to implement the European framework for Threat Intelligence-Based Ethical Red teaming
items.officialTitle: TIBER-EU (2025)
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · financial sector · incident response
items.summary: TIBER-EU is the European method, developed by the ECB with the national central banks, for testing an organisation’s defences with a simulated but realistic attack carried out by ethical hackers (the “red team”) on the live production systems that support its critical or important functions. The attack scenario comes from bespoke threat intelligence that identifies who might target the organisation and with which tactics, techniques and procedures. The test has three phases: preparation (initiation, scoping of the functions to target, procurement of threat intelligence and red team providers), testing (targeted threat intelligence report, scenarios, then the actual attack) and closure (red team and defenders’ reports, a joint replay of the attack, a purple teaming exercise, the remediation plan and a final attestation). Five teams take part: the defenders (the “blue team”, unaware of the test), the threat intelligence provider, the red team, a small internal control team that runs the test in secret and the authority’s team that oversees it. The outcome is not a pass or fail but a picture of the weaknesses to fix.

It sets out the procedures of the national cybersecurity authority, including the identification of essential and important entities, the annual inspection plan and inspections, the information security supervisor, cybersecurity certification and vulnerability assessments. Finally, it organises national coordination: the cybersecurity commissioner, the National Cybersecurity Working Group with its operational staff, forum and sub-groups, crisis management, reporting of large-scale incidents, the single point of contact and the EU peer review.

Conformity is shown by CE marking, with stricter assessments for important and critical products.

items.officialTitle: Décret n° 2-24-921 du 18 rabii II 1446 (22 octobre 2024) relatif au recours aux prestataires de services Cloud par les entités et les infrastructures d'importance vitale disposant de systèmes d'information ou de données sensibles
items.topic: Cybersecurity · cloud · critical infrastructure · supply chain · certification
items.summary: The decree implements the Cybersecurity Law 05-20 for the use of cloud services by entities and critical infrastructure. For sensitive information systems these bodies must use a qualified level 1 cloud provider, with hosting and management systems located in Morocco; for sensitive data, a level 2 provider, which must also process and store data only within the country, be majority Moroccan-owned and employ Moroccan staff. Qualification is granted by the national authority (DGSSI) for up to five years after an assessment against a technical reference framework, and qualified providers are subject to audits. As a transitional measure a non-qualified provider may be used if the service is not available from qualified ones, subject to a risk analysis.

items.title: CMMC Program (32 CFR Part 170)
items.officialTitle: Cybersecurity Maturity Model Certification (CMMC) Program (32 CFR Part 170)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · cyber defence · supply chain · certification
items.summary: The rule establishes the CMMC programme, through which the US Department of Defense checks that its contractors and subcontractors protect Federal Contract Information (FCI) and Controlled Unclassified Information (CUI). It has three levels: Level 1 requires basic safeguarding with an annual self-assessment, Level 2 the 110 requirements of NIST SP 800-171 with a self-assessment or an assessment by an accredited third party (C3PAO), and Level 3 enhanced requirements from NIST SP 800-172 assessed by the government. The required level is set in the contract and becomes a condition of award. A companion rule in the Defense Federal Acquisition Regulation Supplement (DFARS) puts the requirement into solicitations and contracts.

items.officialTitle: EUROCAE ED-202B
items.summary: ED-202B defines the process through which designers and manufacturers of aircraft and airborne equipment show, during certification, that the aircraft is protected against intentional unauthorised electronic interaction (IUEI) that could affect its safety. It sets out the activities to perform throughout development: defining the security scope, assessing risk, identifying protection measures, verifying their effectiveness and documenting all this for the authority. It is the document that states “what” to do, while ED-203A explains the methods. Together with the other standards of the family it is recognised by EASA in AMC 20-42 as an acceptable means of compliance.

items.title: CYBER; Cyber Security for Consumer Internet of Things: Baseline Requirements
items.officialTitle: ETSI EN 303 645
items.summary: The European standard sets baseline security requirements for internet-connected consumer IoT devices, such as cameras, voice assistants, toys, appliances and home sensors. Its thirteen areas of provisions include no universal default passwords, a vulnerability disclosure policy, secure software updates, secure storage of sensitive data, protected communications, a minimised attack surface and easy deletion of personal data. It underpins labelling and certification schemes in several countries and the UK product security requirements for connected products.

items.title: La méthode EBIOS Risk Manager: le guide
items.officialTitle: EBIOS Risk Manager v1.5
items.summary: EBIOS Risk Manager is the method of ANSSI, the French cybersecurity agency, for assessing and treating the digital risks of an organisation, a project or a product. It combines two approaches, compliance with a baseline of essential security measures and the study of realistic attack scenarios, and involves both executives and technical staff. It runs in five workshops: 1) scope and security baseline (missions, business assets and the supporting assets behind them, feared events and their severity, compliance with the security rules already in place); 2) risk origins (who might attack and with what aim, keeping the most relevant pairs); 3) strategic scenarios (high-level attack paths, including through suppliers and partners, with the threat level of each stakeholder); 4) operational scenarios (the attack techniques against critical supporting assets, with their likelihood); 5) risk treatment (strategy, treatment plan, residual risks and their monitoring). The analysis is repeated in a strategic cycle and in a shorter operational cycle. It is used to manage cyber risk, for the security accreditation of information systems and to set the security level of products and services ahead of certification.

items.title: Post-quantum cryptography standards (ML-KEM, ML-DSA, SLH-DSA)
items.officialTitle: NIST FIPS 203, 204 e 205
items.summary: These are the first three US federal public-key cryptography standards designed to withstand attacks even from a quantum computer, the outcome of the international selection process NIST launched in 2016. FIPS 203 defines ML-KEM, a lattice-based mechanism for establishing shared secret keys (derived from CRYSTALS-Kyber); FIPS 204 defines ML-DSA, a digital signature scheme also based on lattices (from CRYSTALS-Dilithium); FIPS 205 defines SLH-DSA, a hash-based signature scheme (from SPHINCS+), intended as an alternative resting on different security assumptions. Each standard provides several parameter sets with different trade-offs between security and performance. They are the main international reference for the migration to post-quantum cryptography by manufacturers, public bodies and operators.

items.summary: Binding Illinois statute in force since 1 January 2026. It amends the employment article of the Illinois Human Rights Act. It is a civil rights violation for an employer to use AI that has the effect of discriminating on the basis of protected classes in recruitment, hiring, promotion, discipline, discharge, or other terms of employment, or to use zip codes as a proxy for protected classes. Employers must also notify employees when they use AI for these purposes. Approved by the Governor on 9 August 2024.

items.title: Common security requirements for radio equipment
items.summary: The three harmonised European standards turn the cybersecurity obligations of the Radio Equipment Directive (Article 3(3)(d), (e) and (f)) into verifiable requirements; these obligations have applied since 1 August 2025 to smartphones, routers, wearables, connected toys and other radio products. Part 1 covers network protection for all internet-connected devices, part 2 the protection of personal data and privacy, and part 3 fraud protection for devices that process money or monetary value. Each part sets out mechanisms such as access and authentication management, secure updates, protected storage and communications, event logging and resilience, with decision trees to assess how they apply.

items.title: Law 195/2024 – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Legea nr. 195 din 25.07.2024 privind protecția datelor cu caracter personal
items.summary: The law transposes into Moldovan law the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and replaces Law No. 133/2011 on personal data protection. It reproduces the principles, legal bases, data subjects' rights, obligations of controllers and processors (data protection by design, records, impact assessments, data protection officers) and rules on transfers abroad. The National Center for Personal Data Protection remains the supervisory authority, with corrective and sanctioning powers. Controllers must notify personal data breaches to the Center without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours. Fines reach 2 million lei or, for undertakings, 2% of total turnover and also apply to public authorities, but are phased in: 10% of the amount in the first year, 40% in the second and 100% from the third.

items.regulator: House of Peoples' Representatives of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia
items.title: Proclamation 1321/2024 – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Personal Data Protection Proclamation No. 1321/2024
items.summary: It is Ethiopia's first general law on personal data protection. It sets out the processing principles, legal bases, rules on sensitive data and data subjects' rights (information, access, rectification, erasure, objection, limits on automated decisions) and designates the Ethiopian Communications Authority as supervisory authority. Controllers and processors must register with the Authority, take security measures and store personal data collected locally on servers in Ethiopia; transfers to countries without adequate protection are prohibited save for exceptions. Controllers must notify personal data breaches to the Authority and communicate them to data subjects within 72 hours of becoming aware of them. Violations carry administrative and criminal fines and up to ten years' imprisonment; for institutions, sensitive data or minors' data the fine can reach 4% of worldwide turnover of the preceding financial year.

items.title: Agreements on Huawei and ZTE components in 5G (Germany)
items.officialTitle: Öffentlich-rechtliche Verträge des Bundes mit Telekom, Vodafone und Telefónica über kritische Komponenten von Huawei und ZTE in den 5G-Netzen
items.topic: Cybersecurity · critical infrastructure · supply chain · telecommunications
items.summary: The Federal Republic of Germany concluded public-law contracts with the mobile operators Telekom, Vodafone and Telefónica, closing the administrative proceedings that the Federal Ministry of the Interior had opened under Section 9b(4) of the BSI Act as then in force, which allowed it to prohibit the use of critical components where the manufacturer is not trustworthy. Under the contracts the operators undertake to stop using critical Huawei and ZTE components in their 5G core networks by the end of 2026 at the latest. By the end of 2029 they must also replace the critical functions of Huawei and ZTE 5G network management systems in their access and transport networks with solutions from other manufacturers. The network areas are defined according to the 3GPP standards.

items.title: Law 014-2024/ALT on information systems security
items.officialTitle: Loi n° 014-2024/ALT du 09 juillet 2024 portant sécurité des systèmes d'information au Burkina Faso
items.topic: Cybersecurity · governance · critical infrastructure · public administration · certification
items.summary: The Law sets the rules on the security of information systems in Burkina Faso in order to control and protect them, identify and manage security risks and incidents, reduce their consequences and regulate the actors involved in securing systems. It applies to the systems of public administration and of bodies with critical infrastructure, including those of military or cyber-defence interest, to electronic communications operators and trust service providers, to natural and legal persons with an economic, social or security impact on the country, and to entities providing support and maintenance for information systems. Among other things it defines security audits, accreditation and the technical approval of providers.

items.title: Cyber Security Act 2024 (Act 854)
items.officialTitle: Cyber Security Act 2024 (Act 854)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · critical infrastructure · governance · incident response · incident reporting · certification
items.summary: The Act establishes the National Cyber Security Committee and gives powers to the national agency NACSA and its Chief Executive. For national critical information infrastructure (NCII) it designates sector leads and the entities operating it, which must follow codes of practice, carry out a risk assessment at least once a year and an audit at least every two years. NCII incidents must be notified immediately by electronic means to the sector lead and NACSA, with details within six hours and full information within fourteen days. The Act also introduces a mandatory licence for providers of managed SOC monitoring and penetration testing services.

items.regulator: Department of Commerce, Bureau of Industry and Security
items.title: ICTS ban on Kaspersky (US Commerce, 2024)
items.officialTitle: Final Determination: Case No. ICTS-2021-002, Kaspersky Lab, Inc.
items.summary: Final determination signed on 14 June 2024 by Secretary of Commerce Gina M. Raimondo under Executive Order 13873 on securing the information and communications technology and services (ICTS) supply chain and 15 CFR part 7. The Department of Commerce found that the provision to US persons of cybersecurity and anti-virus software by Kaspersky Lab, Inc. and its affiliates, subsidiaries and parent companies, including through third parties that integrate it into their products, poses undue and unacceptable risks to US national security. From 20 July 2024 Kaspersky may not enter into new agreements with US persons for these products and services, and from 29 September 2024 it may no longer provide anti-virus signature and codebase updates or operate the Kaspersky Security Network (KSN) in the United States. From the same date the resale, integration into other products and licensing of Kaspersky software in the United States or by US persons are prohibited. Violations are subject to civil and criminal penalties.

items.officialTitle: Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 laying down harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Artificial Intelligence Act)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · artificial intelligence · certification · supply chain
items.summary: The AI Act regulates artificial intelligence systems with a risk-based approach: it bans certain practices and sets obligations for high-risk systems and general-purpose AI models. High-risk systems must achieve accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity (Article 15), including against attacks such as data poisoning or adversarial inputs, alongside risk management, data governance and transparency. Products that comply with the Cyber Resilience Act are presumed to meet the AI Act's cybersecurity requirements.

items.title: FTC Health Breach Notification Rule (2024)
items.officialTitle: Health Breach Notification Rule (16 CFR Part 318), as amended in 2024
items.topic: Cybersecurity · health · data protection · incident reporting
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission rule requires vendors of personal health records and PHR related entities that are not covered by HIPAA, such as many health and wellness apps, to notify breaches of unsecured identifiable health information. Affected individuals must be notified without unreasonable delay and no later than 60 calendar days after discovery; where at least 500 people are affected the FTC must be notified at the same time, otherwise through an annual log, and where at least 500 residents of a State are affected prominent media outlets must also be notified. The 2024 amendments clarify that the rule covers developers of health apps, that a breach of security includes unauthorized disclosures and not only cybersecurity intrusions, allow notice by email and expand the content of the notice. Violations are subject to civil penalties as violations of an FTC rule on unfair or deceptive practices.

items.title: SEC Regulation S-P amendments (2024)
items.officialTitle: Regulation S-P: Privacy of Consumer Financial Information and Safeguarding Customer Information (SEC Release No. 34-100155)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · financial sector · data protection · incident reporting
items.summary: The SEC amendments to Regulation S-P require broker-dealers, investment companies, registered investment advisers, funding portals and transfer agents to adopt written policies and procedures for an incident response program to detect, respond to and recover from unauthorized access to or use of customer information. Where sensitive customer information was, or is reasonably likely to have been, accessed or used without authorization, affected individuals must be notified as soon as practicable and no later than 30 days after the institution becomes aware of the incident, unless a reasonable investigation finds no likely risk of substantial harm or inconvenience; the Attorney General may request a delay on national security or public safety grounds. Covered institutions must oversee their service providers, which must notify them within 72 hours of a breach affecting a customer information system they maintain. The amendments also extend the safeguards and disposal rules to transfer agents and to a broader scope of information, and require written records documenting compliance.

items.title: Decree No. DCLVII – Data protection regulation
items.officialTitle: Decreto della Pontificia Commissione per lo Stato della Città del Vaticano con il quale viene promulgato il Regolamento Generale sulla protezione dei Dati personali
items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · governance · public administration
items.summary: The decree promulgates, on an experimental basis for three years, Vatican City State's first general regulation on personal data protection, which follows the principles and tools of the GDPR. The controller is the Governorate, represented by its Secretary General; its directorates and offices act as processors and appoint contact persons who apply the security measures and keep the records of processing. The regulation governs the legal bases for processing, consent, special categories of data, information notices and the rights of access, rectification, erasure, portability, objection and restriction. The data protection officer's functions are assigned to the General Counsellor of the State, who acts with full independence, examines data subjects' complaints and proposes to the President of the Governorate the order deciding them. Contact persons must report personal data breaches to the processor and the data protection officer within 72 hours of becoming aware of them.

items.title: PAFACA – Foreign adversary controlled apps (TikTok)
items.officialTitle: Protecting Americans from Foreign Adversary Controlled Applications Act (Division H of Public Law 118-50)
items.summary: The Act, enacted on 24 April 2024, makes it unlawful to distribute, maintain or update a "foreign adversary controlled application" in the United States through an online mobile application store or other marketplace, or to provide internet hosting services that enable this. It names applications operated directly or indirectly by ByteDance, Ltd., TikTok and their subsidiaries and successors, and allows the President to designate applications of other companies controlled by a foreign adversary country (China, Russia, Iran or North Korea) that present a significant threat to national security. The prohibitions apply from 19 January 2025, 270 days after enactment, and cease to apply after a "qualified divestiture" that ends foreign adversary control and any operational relationship, including cooperation on the recommendation algorithm and data sharing. Violations are subject to civil penalties of up to $5,000 per US user, enforced by the Attorney General; individual users cannot be penalised.

items.title: CIRCIA – Proposed reporting rule (2024)
items.officialTitle: Cyber Incident Reporting for Critical Infrastructure Act (CIRCIA) Reporting Requirements (Notice of Proposed Rulemaking)
items.summary: The proposed rule through which CISA intends to implement CIRCIA would create a new 6 CFR Part 226. Covered entities are organisations in a critical infrastructure sector that exceed the Small Business Administration's small business size standard or meet sector-based criteria (for example chemical facilities, communications providers, hospitals, IT providers to the federal government, nuclear plants, transportation, and water systems serving more than 3,300 people). They would have to report covered cyber incidents to CISA within 72 hours of reasonably believing they occurred and ransom payments within 24 hours of disbursement, submit supplemental reports promptly, and preserve incident data for at least two years. Where reports are not made, CISA could issue requests for information and subpoenas and refer cases to the Department of Justice. CISA estimates about 316,000 covered entities and a cost of 2.6 billion dollars over the analysis period.

items.title: ED 24-02 – Compromise of Microsoft corporate email
items.officialTitle: ED 24-02: Mitigating the Significant Risk from Nation-State Compromise of Microsoft Corporate Email System
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · supply chain · incident response
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 2 April 2024 after Midnight Blizzard, a Russian state-sponsored cyber actor, compromised Microsoft corporate email accounts and exfiltrated correspondence between federal civilian agencies and Microsoft, using the information obtained, including authentication details shared by email, to try to access customer systems. It applied to agencies whose correspondence with Microsoft had been exfiltrated. Agencies notified by Microsoft of compromised credentials had to remediate tokens, passwords, API keys and other credentials immediately and, by 30 April 2024, reset credentials in associated applications, deactivate unused applications and review sign-in and activity logs. items.title: Common Vulnerability Scoring System version 4.0: Specification Document
items.officialTitle: CVSS v4.0
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · incident response · software security
items.summary: CVSS is the open method, maintained by FIRST, for measuring how severe a software, hardware or firmware vulnerability is and communicating it with a score from 0 to 10 and a string (the “vector”) that summarises the values chosen. Version 4.0 arranges the metrics in four groups: base (the vulnerability’s own characteristics, that is how easy it is to exploit and what impact it has on the confidentiality, integrity and availability of the vulnerable system and of connected systems), threat (for example whether exploit code exists or the vulnerability is already being exploited), environmental (how important the system is and which defences the assessing organisation has in place) and supplemental (extra information such as physical safety or whether the attack can be automated, which does not change the score). The score maps to a qualitative scale: none, low, medium, high, critical. Vendors and vulnerability databases use it to publish the severity of each vulnerability, and organisations use it to decide which ones to fix first.
