items.title: BOD 23-02 – Internet-exposed management interfaces
items.officialTitle: BOD 23-02: Mitigating the Risk from Internet-Exposed Management Interfaces
items.summary: Binding operational directive issued by CISA on 13 June 2023, because threat actors increasingly target network devices and the risk grows when their management interfaces are reachable from the internet. It covers routers, switches, firewalls, VPN concentrators, proxies, load balancers and out-of-band server management interfaces (such as iLO and iDRAC) whose interfaces are internet-accessible over remote management protocols such as HTTP, HTTPS, SSH, Telnet, SNMP, RDP or SMB. Within 14 days of CISA notification or discovery, federal civilian agencies must remove the interface from the internet, making it reachable only from the internal network, or, preferably, protect it with zero trust access controls through a separate policy enforcement point. They must then ensure the same protection for all existing and new devices. Management interfaces of cloud services are excluded.

items.title: Zero Trust Maturity Model, Version 2.0

items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · public administration · governance · digital identity
items.summary: The CISA model is a roadmap for federal civilian agencies moving to a zero trust architecture, as required by Executive Order 14028; CISA also encourages other organisations to use it. It is structured around five pillars (identity, devices, networks, applications and workloads, data) and three cross-cutting capabilities (visibility and analytics, automation and orchestration, governance). For each pillar it describes four maturity stages: traditional, initial, advanced and optimal, so that each organisation can assess where it stands and progress step by step, possibly at a different pace for each pillar. It reflects the seven zero trust tenets of NIST SP 800-207 and is aligned with OMB memorandum M-22-09 on the federal zero trust strategy.

The notice is an early alert given by email, telephone or other means prescribed by the NCUA, and no detailed incident assessment is required within the 72 hours. Events performed in good faith at the request of the system's owner or operator, such as commissioned security testing, are not reportable.

items.summary: Enacted as the Cybersecurity Order 2023 and republished in the 2024 revised edition as the Cybersecurity Act (Chapter 272), this is Brunei's framework law on cybersecurity. It establishes the Commissioner of Cybersecurity, appointed by the Minister with the consent of the Sultan, who administers the Act, designates critical information infrastructure, issues codes of practice and standards of performance and may give binding written directions. Owners of critical information infrastructure must report prescribed cybersecurity incidents within the prescribed period, have a compliance audit carried out at least every two years, conduct a yearly risk assessment and take part in cybersecurity exercises. The direction sets the milestones for removing Huawei from UK networks: no Huawei 5G equipment procured after 31 December 2020, no new installation in 5G networks, no Huawei equipment at sites significant to national security after 28 January 2023 and none in core network functions after 31 December 2023. Huawei's share of 5G access and full-fibre networks is capped at 35% from 2023, its high data rate transmission equipment must leave core networks by 31 December 2025 and all Huawei equipment and services must leave 5G networks by 31 December 2027. The reasoning cites cyber attacks attributed to the Chinese state, Chinese laws allowing the state to require companies to carry out harmful activities, the quality of Huawei's products and the effect of US sanctions on its supply chain.

At CISA's request, agencies must start discovery and enumeration within 72 hours and provide results within 7 days. The directive supports Executive Order 14028.

items.officialTitle: Personal Data Protection Act, No. 9 of 2022
items.summary: It is Sri Lanka's general personal data protection law, amended in 2025. It sets the principles of lawful processing (legal bases, purpose limitation, minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity and confidentiality, transparency and accountability), data subjects' rights and the obligations of controllers and processors (data protection officers, impact assessments, transfers abroad), and establishes the Data Protection Authority. In the event of a personal data breach the controller must notify the Authority in the form, manner and time set by the Authority's rules; the Act sets no deadline in hours. The Authority can impose penalties of up to 10 million rupees per contravention. Commencement is phased: the provisions on the Authority have operated since 2023, the processing and controller obligations apply from 1 January 2027, while data subjects' rights and penalties still await a ministerial order.

items.title: FCC 22-22 – Pacific Networks and ComNet revocation
items.officialTitle: Pacific Networks Corp. and ComNet (USA) LLC – Order on Revocation and Termination
items.summary: Order adopted by the Federal Communications Commission on 16 March 2022 and released on 23 March 2022, which revokes the domestic authority and revokes and terminates the international authority of Pacific Networks Corp. and its wholly owned subsidiary ComNet (USA) LLC under section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934. The Commission found that the two companies, US subsidiaries of a Chinese state-owned entity, are subject to exploitation, influence and control by the Chinese government and that keeping the authorisations would give them, their parent entities and the Chinese government opportunities to access, monitor, store and in some cases disrupt or misroute US communications. It also found that their conduct and representations to the FCC and Congress showed a lack of trustworthiness and that no mitigation could address the risks. The companies had to discontinue all services provided under section 214 within 60 days, at the end of which the FCC reclaimed the two international signalling point codes (ISPCs) assigned to ComNet.

items.title: Law 1/10 of 2022 on cybercrime
items.officialTitle: Loi n°1/10 du 16 mars 2022 portant prévention et répression de la cybercriminalité au Burundi
items.topic: Cybersecurity · cybercrime · telecommunications · critical infrastructure · data protection
items.summary: The law punishes computer offences committed in Burundi, or abroad with effects in the country, and offences that require electronic evidence to be gathered, including attacks on the computer systems of critical infrastructure. It requires network operators and service providers to ensure the security of their services, keep connection and traffic data for at least ten years, monitor traffic on their networks, run a management centre for their critical infrastructure in the country and install video surveillance in internet cafés. Service providers must inform customers of risks, report straight away to investigators any use of their networks to commit offences and block illegal content when the authorities ask. The law defines offences against systems and data (illegal access, interception, damage, payment card fraud), content offences (pornography and grooming of minors, racism and xenophobia, threats, spreading rumours, insults), attacks on state security and on privacy, with prison terms up to life and heavy fines. It also governs the expedited preservation of data, the seizure of systems and the real-time collection of traffic and content data.

Transfers outside Oman follow the rules of the Regulation, and violations carry fines of up to OMR 500,000.

items.regulator: Parliament of the United Republic of Tanzania
items.title: Personal Data Protection Act 2022
items.officialTitle: Sheria ya Ulinzi wa Taarifa Binafsi, 2022 (Sheria Na. 11 ya 2022)
items.summary: It is Tanzania's general personal data protection law and applies to Mainland Tanzania and to Tanzania Zanzibar, where it does not cover non-union matters. It sets the principles of processing and rules on the collection, use, disclosure, retention and correction of data, prohibits the processing of sensitive personal data save for exceptions, and allows transfers abroad to countries with adequate protection or in specified cases. It establishes the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC), which registers data controllers and processors, monitors compliance, handles complaints and cooperates with foreign authorities. Anyone collecting or processing personal data must register with the Commission (registration lasts five years and public institutions are deemed registered), appoint a data protection officer and adopt a code of ethics or policy to be approved by the Commission. The data controller must notify the Commission, without undue delay, of any security breach affecting personal data. Data subjects have the rights of access, to prevent harmful processing and direct marketing, not to be subject to solely automated decisions, to rectification and erasure, and to compensation. The Commission may impose administrative fines of up to 100 million shillings; unlawful disclosure of data is punishable by fines of up to 20 million shillings or up to ten years' imprisonment for individuals and by fines of up to 5 billion shillings for companies.

items.title: ED 22-02 – Apache Log4j vulnerability
items.officialTitle: ED 22-02: Mitigate Apache Log4j Vulnerability
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · software security · incident response
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 17 December 2021 on the series of vulnerabilities in the Apache Log4j library, including CVE-2021-44228. It applied to federal agency applications in any information system, including cloud and third-party hosted systems, giving priority to solution stacks that accept data input from the internet. By 5 pm on 23 December 2021 agencies had to identify those stacks, check their software against the affected-software database published by CISA on GitHub and, for each vulnerable asset, apply the patch, adopt one of the mitigations listed by CISA or remove it from the network. They also had to assume compromise of every stack containing affected software and hunt for post-exploitation activity, such as outbound JNDI LDAP/RMI traffic. A report on each affected application was due to CISA by 28 December 2021. CISA closed the directive on 8 April 2022, transferring its requirements to BOD 22-01.

items.title: FTC Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314)
items.officialTitle: Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information (FTC Safeguards Rule, 16 CFR Part 314), as amended in 2021 and 2023
items.topic: Cybersecurity · financial sector · data protection · incident reporting
items.summary: The Federal Trade Commission's Safeguards Rule implements the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and requires financial institutions under FTC jurisdiction, such as mortgage brokers, check cashers, tax preparers, car dealers that lease vehicles and finders, to maintain a written information security program for customer information. The 2021 amendments specify the content of the program: a Qualified Individual, a written risk assessment, access controls, a systems inventory, encryption of data in transit and at rest, multi-factor authentication, secure disposal, monitoring, annual penetration testing and six-monthly vulnerability assessments, service provider oversight, a written incident response plan and at least an annual report to the board of directors. Institutions holding information on fewer than 5,000 consumers are exempt from some of these requirements. The 2023 amendment requires notifying the FTC as soon as possible, and no later than 30 days after discovery, of the unauthorized acquisition of unencrypted information of at least 500 consumers.

items.officialTitle: China Telecom (Americas) Corporation – Order on Revocation and Termination
items.summary: Order adopted unanimously by the Federal Communications Commission on 26 October 2021 and released on 2 November 2021, which revokes the domestic authority and revokes and terminates the international authorisations of China Telecom (Americas) Corporation (CTA), the US subsidiary of the Chinese state-owned China Telecom, under section 214 of the Communications Act of 1934. The Commission found that CTA is subject to exploitation, influence and control by the Chinese government and highly likely to be forced to comply with its requests, and that keeping the authorisations would give it opportunities to access, store, disrupt or misroute US communications, creating national security and law enforcement risks that no further mitigation could address. It also found that the company's conduct and representations to the FCC and other agencies showed a lack of candour and trustworthiness. CTA had to discontinue all services provided under section 214 within 60 days.

items.summary: It is Rwanda's general law on the protection of personal data and privacy. It sets processing principles, consent, rules on sensitive data and children, data subjects' rights and the obligations of controllers and processors, who must register with the supervisory authority and in certain cases designate a data protection officer. The supervisory authority is the public authority in charge of cyber security (the National Cyber Security Authority). Personal data must be stored in Rwanda unless a registration certificate authorises storage abroad. Controllers must communicate personal data breaches to the authority within 48 hours and submit a report within 72 hours; processors must alert the controller within 48 hours. Administrative fines reach 1% of global turnover, and some offences carry imprisonment and, for legal entities, fines of up to 5% of annual turnover.

items.summary: It is Saudi Arabia's first general personal data protection law and applies to any processing in the Kingdom of personal data relating to individuals, including deceased persons, and to processing outside the Kingdom of the data of individuals residing there. It grants the rights to be informed, to access and obtain a copy of one's data and to request its correction and destruction, and as a rule makes processing subject to consent, with exceptions and stricter rules for sensitive, health and credit data and for marketing; transfers abroad are allowed for listed purposes if they do not prejudice national security and the destination ensures adequate protection, under a dedicated regulation. Controllers must assess the impact of processing, notify the competent authority of personal data breaches (within 72 hours under the Implementing Regulation) and inform data subjects when a breach may harm them; the Regulations determine when a data protection officer must be appointed. The competent authority is the Saudi Data and AI Authority (SDAIA), which receives complaints and runs the national register of controllers. Unlawfully disclosing or publishing sensitive data to harm the data subject or for personal benefit is punishable by up to two years' imprisonment and a fine of up to SAR 3 million; other violations carry a warning or a fine of up to SAR 5 million, which may be doubled for repeat offences.

It inserts definitions of personal data, cyberspace, cyber resource, malware and cyber attack, and a new chapter on personal data protection: those responsible for managing personal data must keep and protect it according to its type and security level, may not disclose, distribute or alter it without the data subject's consent or a legal basis, may not use it for other purposes and must destroy it once the set period expires. These rules do not apply to prevention, investigation and intelligence activities of the designated authorities in the fields of cybersecurity, crime and national security. New offences punish the unlawful management and unauthorised use of personal data (one to three years' imprisonment and fines of up to 10 million kyat), spreading false news to cause public panic or division, and cyber attacks against the state's sovereignty, security or international relations (up to seven years).

items.officialTitle: Cybercrime Act 2021 (Act No. 3 of 2021)
items.summary: The Act introduces a cybercrime framework in Fiji modelled on the Budapest Convention and replaces the computer offences in sections 336 to 346 of the Crimes Act 2009. It punishes unauthorised access, interception, acts impairing data and systems, supplying or possessing tools to commit these offences, computer-related forgery, fraud and extortion, identity theft and theft of telecommunication services, with fines and imprisonment of up to 10 years for individuals and higher fines for bodies corporate. It sets out investigative powers: search and seizure, expedited preservation of stored computer data and traffic data, production orders, real-time collection of traffic data and interception of content data; it also punishes disclosing an investigation and failing to provide the assistance required. It governs international cooperation, including extradition, mutual assistance and transborder access to data, and provides for a 24/7 point of contact designated by the Minister.

items.title: ED 21-01 – SolarWinds Orion code compromise
items.officialTitle: ED 21-01: Mitigate SolarWinds Orion Code Compromise
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · supply chain · incident response
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 13 December 2020 after the compromise of SolarWinds Orion code, versions 2019.4 through 2020.2.1 HF1, activity later attributed by the US government to the Russian Foreign Intelligence Service (SVR). Federal agencies had to take forensic images of affected systems where they had the capability, immediately disconnect or power down Orion products, block external traffic, remove threat actor accounts and persistence mechanisms and, by 12 pm on 14 December 2020, report indicators of compromise and submit a status report attested by the CIO. Supplemental guidance issued in December 2020 and January 2021 clarified the affected versions, sorted networks into three categories and set 12 conditions for agencies accepting the risk of running Orion. Supplemental Direction V4 of 22 April 2021 required networks with follow-on threat actor activity to carry out eviction instructions by 16 July 2021.

items.title: IoT Cybersecurity Improvement Act of 2020
items.officialTitle: Internet of Things Cybersecurity Improvement Act of 2020 (Public Law 116-207)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · iot · public administration · supply chain
items.summary: The Act sets minimum security requirements for Internet of Things (IoT) devices owned or controlled by the United States federal government. It directs NIST to publish standards and guidelines on agencies' use and management of IoT devices, covering secure development, identity management, patching and configuration management, to be reviewed at least every five years, and OMB to align agency information security policies with them, excluding national security systems. NIST must also publish guidelines on reporting and resolving security vulnerabilities in federal information systems, which also apply to contractors and subcontractors, aligned with ISO/IEC 29147 and 30111. From 4 December 2022 agencies may not procure, renew contracts for or use IoT devices that prevent compliance with these rules, unless a waiver is granted for national security, research or alternative security measures.

items.title: ED 20-04 – Netlogon vulnerability
items.officialTitle: ED 20-04: Mitigate Netlogon Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability from August 2020 Patch Tuesday
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · digital identity · software security
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 18 September 2020 on vulnerability CVE-2020-1472 in the Microsoft Windows Netlogon Remote Protocol (MS-NRPC), a core Active Directory authentication component, which lets an unauthenticated attacker with network access to a domain controller completely compromise Active Directory identity services. The update released by Microsoft on 11 August 2020 was the only mitigation, other than removing domain controllers from the network. By 11:59 PM on Monday 21 September 2020 federal agencies had to apply the update to all Windows Servers with the domain controller role, or remove them, and put in place controls so that new or reconnected domain controllers were updated before joining agency networks. By 23 September they had to send CISA a CIO-attested completion report. For externally hosted servers the provider was responsible unless the domain controller was within the agency's authorisation boundary.

items.title: BOD 20-01 – Vulnerability disclosure policy
items.officialTitle: BOD 20-01: Develop and Publish a Vulnerability Disclosure Policy
items.summary: Binding operational directive issued by CISA on 2 September 2020 in support of OMB M-20-32 on improving vulnerability identification, management and remediation. It requires federal executive branch agencies to publish, within 180 days, a vulnerability disclosure policy (VDP) at the /vulnerability-disclosure-policy path of their primary .gov website and to put in place procedures for handling reports. The policy must state which systems are in scope, the types of testing allowed and prohibited, how to submit reports, including anonymously, and a commitment not to pursue legal action against good-faith research; it may not require personal data or limit testing to US citizens or vetted parties. Its scope must be extended step by step until, within two years, it covers all internet-accessible systems. Agencies report vulnerabilities in commercial products to CISA and submit regular metrics through CyberScope.

items.title: ED 20-03 – Windows DNS Server vulnerability
items.officialTitle: ED 20-03: Mitigate Windows DNS Server Remote Code Execution Vulnerability from July 2020 Patch Tuesday
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 16 July 2020 on vulnerability CVE-2020-1350 in Windows Servers configured with the DNS Server role, fixed by Microsoft on 14 July 2020, which lets an unauthenticated attacker run code in the context of the Local System Account by sending malicious requests to the DNS server. Although no active exploitation was known, CISA judged that the flaw could be reverse engineered from the public patch. By 2 pm on 17 July 2020 agencies had to apply the July update or a temporary registry workaround to all servers running the DNS role, and by 24 July update all Windows Servers, remove the registry workaround and put in place controls so that new or reconnected servers were updated before joining agency networks. An initial status report was due on 20 July and a CIO-attested completion report on 24 July. CISA recommended removing servers that could not be updated within 7 business days.

items.title: ED 20-02 – Windows vulnerabilities, January 2020
items.officialTitle: ED 20-02: Mitigate Windows Vulnerabilities from January 2020 Patch Tuesday
items.topic: Cybersecurity · public administration · cryptography · software security
items.summary: Emergency directive issued by CISA on 14 January 2020 on the vulnerabilities fixed by Microsoft's January 2020 security updates: CVE-2020-0601, a flaw in elliptic curve cryptography (ECC) certificate validation in Windows 10, Server 2016 and Server 2019, and CVE-2020-0609, CVE-2020-0610 and CVE-2020-0611, affecting the Remote Desktop client and RD Gateway Server. According to its FAQ, the directive applied to all vulnerabilities in the January update. By 5 pm on 29 January 2020 federal civilian agencies had to apply the updates to all affected endpoints, including servers, IoT devices and virtual machines, and put in place controls so that new or reconnected endpoints were patched before joining agency networks. An initial status report was due within three business days and a CIO-signed completion report by 29 January. CISA recommended removing endpoints that could not be patched within 10 business days.

items.title: Privacy Act 2020
items.officialTitle: Privacy Act 2020
items.summary: New Zealand's general privacy law, which replaced the Privacy Act 1993 and applies to public and private agencies. It is built on thirteen information privacy principles covering the collection, storage and security, access, correction, accuracy, retention, use and disclosure of personal information, disclosure outside New Zealand (only to agencies with comparable protection or with the individual's informed authorisation) and unique identifiers; since 1 May 2026 principle 3A requires agencies to tell people when their information is collected from another source. Privacy breaches that have caused or are likely to cause serious harm must be notified to the Privacy Commissioner and to the affected people as soon as practicable, and failing to notify the Commissioner is an offence. The Commissioner can issue binding codes of practice, compliance notices and binding access directions; offences such as impersonating someone to obtain their information, destroying requested documents or ignoring a compliance notice carry fines of up to NZ$10,000. The Act also applies to overseas businesses carrying on business in New Zealand.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2019
items.officialTitle: Data Protection Act, 2019 (No. 24 of 2019)
items.summary: It is Kenya's general personal data protection law and gives effect to Article 31(c) and (d) of the Constitution on the right to privacy. It establishes the Office of the Data Protection Commissioner (ODPC) and applies to data controllers and processors established or ordinarily resident in Kenya and to foreign ones processing personal data of data subjects located in the country. Controllers and processors must register with the Data Commissioner according to the thresholds the Commissioner sets, and may appoint a data protection officer. The law sets the principles of processing, the lawful bases, data protection impact assessments, rules for children's data and direct marketing, conditions for sensitive personal data and the rights to information, access, objection, rectification, erasure and portability. Transfers abroad require appropriate safeguards proven to the Data Commissioner or one of the listed necessities; sensitive data also requires the data subject's consent, and the government may require certain processing to take place on servers or data centres located in Kenya. Where a breach creates a real risk of harm to data subjects, the controller must notify the Data Commissioner without delay and within 72 hours and inform the data subjects in writing; processors must alert the controller within 48 hours. The Data Commissioner may issue enforcement notices and penalties of up to 5 million shillings or, for undertakings, up to 1% of annual turnover, whichever is lower; offences carry fines of up to 3 million shillings or up to ten years' imprisonment.

items.summary: Niger's cybercrime law, adopted to implement the 2011 ECOWAS directive and modelled on the Budapest Convention; in the absence of a cybersecurity framework law or a published strategy, it is the country's main legal text on the subject. items.title: BOD 19-02 – Vulnerability remediation for internet systems
items.officialTitle: BOD 19-02: Vulnerability Remediation Requirements for Internet-Accessible Systems
items.summary: Binding operational directive issued by CISA on 29 April 2019 that superseded and revoked BOD 15-01 of 2015, which required critical vulnerabilities on internet-facing systems flagged by the weekly Cyber Hygiene scans to be remediated within 30 days; BOD 19-02 extended the requirement to high vulnerabilities. Federal agencies had to remove Cyber Hygiene scanning IP addresses from block lists, notify CISA within five working days of any change to their internet-accessible IP addresses, and remediate critical vulnerabilities within 15 calendar days and high ones within 30 days of initial detection. For vulnerabilities not remediated in time they had to return within three working days a remediation plan with constraints, interim mitigations and an estimated completion date. CISA verified compliance through persistent scanning and engaged agency leadership when deadlines were missed. It was revoked and superseded by BOD 26-04 of 10 June 2026.

items.summary: San Marino's personal data protection law closely follows the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and repeals Law No. 70 of 1995, which remains in force only for data on legal persons. It covers principles, legal bases, children's consent from age 16, data subjects' rights, obligations of controllers and processors (records, impact assessments, data protection officers) and transfers to third countries. It establishes the Data Protection Authority (Autorità Garante per la protezione dei dati personali) as independent supervisory authority. Controllers must notify personal data breaches to the Authority without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours. Administrative fines reach 10 million euros or, for undertakings, 4% of annual turnover.

items.topic: Cybersecurity · critical infrastructure · supply chain · telecommunications
items.summary: With this warning, issued under Section 12 of Act No. 181/2014 on cybersecurity, the National Cyber and Information Security Agency (NÚKIB) found that the use of technical or software means of Huawei Technologies Co., Ltd. and ZTE Corporation, including their subsidiaries, is a cybersecurity threat. The reasoning cites the legal and political environment of the People's Republic of China, which requires companies to cooperate with the state, including in intelligence activities, the organisational and personal links between the two companies and the state, and Chinese intelligence activity in the Czech Republic. Bodies and persons required to implement security measures under the act must take the warning into account in their risk assessment, risk treatment plan and supplier selection. The warning does not ban the products outright, but makes it mandatory to weigh this threat in risk management.

items.title: Estonian Personal Data Protection Act (IKS)
items.officialTitle: Isikuandmete kaitse seadus
items.summary: It is the Estonian law implementing the GDPR and transposing Directive (EU) 2016/680 on police and criminal justice processing; it repeals the 2007 Personal Data Protection Act. It sets the age of children's consent to information society services at 13 and lays down specific rules on, among other things, processing for journalistic, academic, artistic and literary purposes, research and statistics with pseudonymised data, data of deceased persons (consent remains valid for ten years after death) and data on debtors' defaults. The independent supervisory authority is the Data Protection Inspectorate (Andmekaitse Inspektsioon), whose director is appointed by the Government for five years after hearing the Riigikogu Constitutional Committee. Infringements of the GDPR are misdemeanours, handled by the Inspectorate and punishable by fines of up to EUR 20 million or, for legal persons, up to 4% of worldwide annual turnover if higher; the Inspectorate can also impose penalty payments up to the same amounts. For processing under the GDPR, breach notification follows Article 33 (72 hours); for police and criminal justice processing the law requires notification to the Inspectorate without delay and, where possible, within 72 hours.

items.summary: The Law sets Togo's cybersecurity framework and the criminal-law protection of the information society. It entrusts the Government, through the ministries for security and the digital economy, with defining national cybersecurity policy and the strategies that implement it, and makes the security ministry the government authority for cybersecurity. It establishes the National Cybersecurity Agency (ANCy), the national authority for the security of essential infrastructure and public authorities' information systems, which designates operators of essential services, sets their protection rules, checks compliance, grants accreditations and may impose sanctions. It creates a Digital Sovereignty Fund. The second part defines computer offences (illegal access, interference with systems and data, child sexual abuse material, racist or xenophobic content, online threats and insults) and their penalties.

items.officialTitle: Tietosuojalaki (1050/2018)
items.summary: Finnish law specifying and supplementing the GDPR and repealing the Personal Data Act of 1999 (henkilötietolaki). It establishes the Data Protection Ombudsman (tietosuojavaltuutettu), an independent authority attached to the Ministry of Justice, with two Deputy Ombudsmen and an expert board, and governs its access and inspection powers. It specifies legal bases for certain processing (including special categories of data, criminal-offence data, research, archiving and statistics), derogations from data subjects' rights and freedom of expression, and sets the age of children's consent to information society services at 13. GDPR administrative fines are imposed by a sanctions board made up of the Ombudsman and the Deputy Ombudsmen and cannot be imposed on state and municipal authorities; data protection offences are punished under the Criminal Code. Breach notification follows Article 33 GDPR (to the Ombudsman within 72 hours).

items.summary: The law adapts Spanish law to the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and repeals Organic Law 15/1999 and Royal Decree-law 5/2018. It regulates children's consent, legal bases for processing based on legal obligations or public interest, certain specific processing (video surveillance, credit information systems, internal whistleblowing systems, marketing), data protection officers and the regime of the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) and the regional authorities. It classifies infringements as very serious, serious and minor, including failure to notify personal data breaches under Articles 33 and 34 GDPR (72 hours); public bodies receive a warning instead of a fine. Title X recognises digital rights such as net neutrality, the right to digital disconnection and privacy in the workplace.

items.summary: It is Serbia's general personal data protection law, modelled on the GDPR and Directive (EU) 2016/680, replacing the 2008 law. items.title: COBIT 2019 Framework
items.officialTitle: COBIT 2019
items.summary: The ISACA framework helps organisations’ leadership govern and manage information and technology so that it creates value while keeping risk and resources under control. It separates governance, which is the board’s responsibility, from management and defines forty governance and management objectives, grouped into five domains, each described in terms of the processes, organisational structures, information, skills, culture and services it requires. The governance system is tailored to the organisation through design factors (strategy, risk profile, size, role of IT, threat landscape) and process capability is measured on a CMMI-based scale. Used by auditors, IT and security managers, it is complemented by focus-area guides, including one on information security.

items.topic: Cybersecurity · cybercrime · critical infrastructure · telecommunications · incident reporting
items.summary: The Law governs the prevention and punishment of cyber crimes in Rwanda. It requires electronic communications service providers to inform their clients of threats and protective measures, set up reporting procedures and immediately report to the cyber security authority when their systems are used to commit offences, preserving information useful for investigations and removing illegal content at the request of the authorities. It leaves to a Presidential Order the minimum rules for the protection of critical information infrastructure. It governs search, seizure, preservation and disclosure of data and the use of forensic methods, and punishes offences against the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data and systems, computer fraud and forgery, content offences such as publishing rumours that may incite fear or violence, terrorism-related offences and failures by service providers, including not reporting cyber threats.

items.officialTitle: قانون رقم 175 لسنة 2018 في شأن مكافحة جرائم تقنية المعلومات
items.summary: The Law, promulgated by the President of the Republic on 14 August 2018, is Egypt's framework against crimes committed through information technology. It requires service providers to retain for 180 days data identifying users, traffic data and terminal equipment data, to keep it confidential and secure and to disclose it only on a reasoned order from a judicial authority. Investigating authorities may order the blocking of websites, including foreign ones, that broadcast content constituting an offence and deemed a threat to national security or the economy, subject to court confirmation within 72 hours. Offences punished with imprisonment and fines include unauthorised access, interception, damage to data and systems, attacks on networks, distribution of attack tools, unauthorised access to payment card data, fake accounts and violations of privacy and family values, with heavier penalties for government systems. Those managing a legal person are liable if they fail to report to the authorities, as soon as they learn of it, an offence affecting the entity's systems.

items.summary: The LGPD is Brazil's general personal data protection law and draws largely on the GDPR. Controllers must report to the ANPD and data subjects security incidents that may cause relevant risk or harm; the ANPD regulation (Resolution CD/ANPD No. 15/2024) sets the deadline at three working days. Fines reach 2% of revenue in Brazil, up to 50 million reais per infringement.

items.summary: It is the Icelandic law giving the GDPR, which applies to Iceland as an EEA State, the force of law in Iceland and containing the national adaptation rules; it replaces Act No. 77/2000 on data protection. The Regulation is published as an annex to the Act, which also applies to matters outside the scope of the EEA Agreement. The Act sets the digital age of consent at 13, allows the use of the national identity number (kennitala) only for a legitimate purpose and where needed for secure identification, and governs, among other things, sensitive data, electronic surveillance and restrictions of data subjects' rights. It confirms Persónuvernd as the independent supervisory authority, with its own board, which can impose administrative fines from ISK 100,000 up to ISK 2.4 billion or 4% of worldwide turnover, including on public authorities; the most serious infringements are punishable by imprisonment of up to three years. items.title: Precautionary measure on Kaspersky (Netherlands)
items.officialTitle: Voorzorgsmaatregel ten aanzien van gebruik Kaspersky antivirussoftware
items.summary: In a letter to the House of Representatives of 14 May 2018, the Minister of Justice and Security announced that the Dutch government had decided, as a precaution, to phase out Kaspersky Lab antivirus software in central government (rijksoverheid). Companies and organisations running vital services and processes and companies subject to the General Security Requirements for Defence Contracts (ABDO) were advised to do the same. The government bases the decision on the broad and deep access to systems that antivirus software has, on Russian legislation requiring companies such as Kaspersky to support the Russian intelligence services, and on Russia's offensive cyber programme, which also targets the Netherlands. Although no concrete cases of misuse are known in the Netherlands, the risk of digital espionage and sabotage cannot be ruled out; the measure covers only the antivirus software and not other Kaspersky products or services.

items.title: STRIDE: threat categories of the Microsoft Threat Modeling Tool
items.officialTitle: STRIDE
items.summary: STRIDE is Microsoft’s threat modelling model, a way of spotting at design time what could go wrong with the security of a piece of software or a system. The name is the acronym of the six threat categories it proposes: Spoofing (pretending to be another user or system, for example with stolen credentials), Tampering (unauthorised changes to data, stored or in transit), Repudiation (denying having performed an action when the system cannot prove it), Information disclosure (exposing information to people who should not see it), Denial of service (making a service unavailable to legitimate users) and Elevation of privilege (gaining privileges one should not have). In practice the system is drawn as a diagram (components, data flows, data stores, trust boundaries) and for each element the question is which of the six categories of threat apply, before choosing countermeasures. Each category matches a security property to protect: authentication, integrity, non-repudiation, confidentiality, availability and authorisation.

items.summary: German federal law supplementing the GDPR, transposing Directive (EU) 2016/680 on processing in criminal matters and replacing the previous 1990 BDSG. Part 1 contains common provisions, including the statute of the Federal Commissioner for Data Protection and Freedom of Information (BfDI), the supervisory authority for federal public bodies, while private bodies are supervised by the authorities of the Länder. Part 2 specifies the GDPR (among other things employee data, video surveillance, credit scoring, data protection officers and restrictions on data subjects' rights); Part 3 governs police and criminal-justice processing, with a duty to notify breaches to the BfDI without undue delay and, where feasible, within 72 hours. Public authorities are not subject to administrative fines; unlawful disclosure or processing of data for gain is a criminal offence punishable by up to three years' imprisonment.

items.title: Austrian Data Protection Act (DSG)
items.officialTitle: Bundesgesetz zum Schutz natürlicher Personen bei der Verarbeitung personenbezogener Daten (Datenschutzgesetz – DSG)
items.summary: It is the Austrian law implementing the GDPR: the 2018 adaptation act renamed and largely rewrote the Data Protection Act 2000, and the text also transposes Directive (EU) 2016/680 on police and criminal justice processing. It keeps the fundamental right to data protection (§ 1) with constitutional rank. It sets the age of children's consent to information society services at 14 and lays down specific rules on, among other things, research, archives and statistics, freedom of expression and journalism, and image recording, including CCTV. The supervisory authority is the Datenschutzbehörde, headed by a director appointed by the Federal President on the Government's proposal for five years; since 2025 a Parliamentary Data Protection Committee has supervised legislative activities. The Datenschutzbehörde imposes the fines under Article 83 GDPR, favouring warnings for first infringements, but may not fine authorities and public bodies; the law also provides for administrative fines of up to EUR 50,000 and a criminal offence punishable by up to one year's imprisonment. Personal data breaches are notified under Article 33 GDPR (72 hours), also for police and criminal justice processing.

items.officialTitle: ກົດໝາຍວ່າດ້ວຍການປົກປ້ອງຂໍ້ມູນເອເລັກໂຕຣນິກ
items.summary: Laos' law on the protection of electronic data, which serves as its general personal data law. It distinguishes general data from specific data (government data and personal data), which may be accessed, used or disclosed only with the consent of the data owner or the competent body. Collection requires informing the data owner of its purpose and content and obtaining consent; data may be kept only as long as necessary, after which personal data must be deleted or made inaccessible unless the law provides otherwise; use, disclosure and transfer to third parties require the owner's consent, and personal and government data may not be sent outside Laos without the owner's consent or a legal basis. Data managers must classify government data by security level, have a unit or staff member responsible for security, keep backups, assess risks, encrypt important data (such as financial and banking data) in transfer and respond to intrusions, if necessary with the help of the national computer emergency response centre. Data owners can access, correct and delete their data and complain when they suffer harm; data managers may not collect, use or disclose data on ethnicity, race, political opinions, religious beliefs, sexual behaviour, criminal records or health. Implementation is led by the Ministry of Post and Telecommunications (now Technology and Communications); violations that are not crimes are fined 15 million kip.

Transfers abroad are allowed to states that ensure data protection, and otherwise only with the data subject's written consent or where treaties or laws provide for them. Operators must take legal, organisational and technical measures to prevent unlawful access, detect it promptly and minimise its consequences, answer data subject requests within one working day and inform data subjects within one working day when their data is passed to third parties. The Cabinet of Ministers sets policy in the field and may create an authority to protect data subjects' rights, while the Prosecutor General supervises compliance.

items.summary: It is Qatar's general personal data protection law and applies to data processed electronically, collected in preparation for electronic processing or processed by a combination of electronic and traditional means. Controllers may process data only with the individual's consent, unless processing is necessary for a legitimate purpose of the controller or of the third party receiving the data; individuals may withdraw consent, object to processing, request erasure or correction of their data and access it. Controllers and processors must take proportionate precautions against loss, damage, alteration, disclosure or unlawful access: processors report any breach to the controller, and controllers must inform the individual and the competent department of the ministry when a breach may cause serious harm to the data or to privacy. Personal data of a special nature (ethnic origin, children, health, religious beliefs, marital status, criminal offences) require a permit from the competent department, websites directed at children must obtain the explicit consent of the child's guardian and direct electronic marketing requires prior consent; conversely, controllers may not restrict cross-border data flows unless the processing breaches the Law or may cause serious harm. Violations carry fines of up to QAR 1 million, or up to QAR 5 million for the security obligations, data of a special nature and children's data.

It also penalises the forgery and destruction of electronic documents and systems, including medical records, online threats and extortion, computer fraud, obstructing access to websites and systems, interception, unauthorised access to credit card data, content contrary to public morals, the use of networks for human trafficking, drug trafficking, money laundering and support for terrorist organisations, as well as online breaches of the press law. Courts may order the confiscation of devices and proceeds and the closure of the premises or website; the representatives of legal persons are liable to the financial penalties where their breach of duty contributed to the offence.

items.title: Digital evidence and incident investigation
items.summary: The four standards cover the whole digital forensics path, from first response at the incident scene to presenting the findings. ISO/IEC 27037 explains how to identify, collect, acquire and preserve potential digital evidence (disks, phones, cameras, networked systems) without altering it and while documenting the chain of custody. They help CSIRTs, corporate investigators, police forces and expert witnesses keep evidence usable in disciplinary or court proceedings, including across jurisdictions.

items.summary: It is Madagascar's general personal data protection law and applies to processing, automated or not, carried out wholly or partly on Malagasy territory by controllers established in the country or using means of processing located there; purely personal activities and journalism are excluded. It sets the principles of processing, a security obligation, the legal bases, a ban on processing sensitive data (including biometric and genetic data) save for exceptions, and rules on transfers abroad, allowed to States with similar protection or with the Commission's authorisation. It grants the rights to information, access, rectification and objection. It establishes the Commission Malagasy de l'Informatique et des Libertés (CMIL), an independent administrative authority with regulatory, inspection and sanctioning powers: processing must be declared before it starts, processing presenting particular risks needs an authorisation and public-sector processing a regulatory act issued after the CMIL's binding opinion. Every controller must appoint a data protection officer, which exempts it from declarations. It contains no specific obligation to notify data breaches. The CMIL may impose fines of up to 5% of turnover excluding tax for the last financial year, doubled for repeat offences; criminal offences carry up to five years' imprisonment and fines of up to 10 million ariary.

items.summary: The Law, passed by the Shura Council and the Council of Representatives and promulgated by the King on 30 September 2014, is Bahrain's statute on information technology crimes. It punishes with imprisonment and fines unauthorised access to systems, damage to data and systems, with penalties doubled where this disrupts public services or endangers life and health, interception, threats of damage for extortion, producing and distributing tools and access codes to commit these offences, computer forgery and fraud, the use of encryption to commit or conceal offences, and online pornography offences, which are more serious where children are involved. It sets processing principles (consent, purpose, quality, security, confidentiality), rules for sensitive data and for the disclosure and international transfer of data, and recognises rights of access, rectification, erasure and objection and the habeas data action. It establishes the Directorate for Personal Data Protection (Dirección de Protección de Datos Personales) within the Ministry of Finance and Public Credit, which keeps the register of data files. Controllers must take security measures; the law does not require breach notification. Sanctions range from a warning to the suspension and closure of the file.

items.title: PDPA 2012 – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Personal Data Protection Act 2012
items.summary: Singapore's general law on the collection, use, disclosure and care of personal data by organisations, which also sets up the national Do Not Call Registry against unwanted telemarketing. It lays down ten main obligations: consent, purpose limitation, notification, access and correction, accuracy, protection, retention limitation, transfer limitation, data breach notification and accountability (internal policies and a data protection officer). Notifiable breaches, meaning those likely to cause significant harm or affecting 500 or more individuals, must be reported to the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) within three calendar days of the assessment that they are notifiable, and to affected individuals where significant harm is likely; data intermediaries alert the organisation without undue delay. The PDPC can issue directions and financial penalties of up to S$1 million or, for organisations with an annual turnover in Singapore above S$10 million, up to 10% of that turnover if higher; its decisions can be appealed to the Data Protection Appeal Panel and individuals have a right of private action. The Act generally does not apply to public agencies, to individuals acting in a personal or domestic capacity or as employees, or to business contact information.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2011
items.officialTitle: Data Protection Act, 2011 (Act No. 5 of 2012)
items.summary: The Act establishes the Data Protection Commission and sets the principles for processing personal information: minimality, collection from the data subject, purpose and retention limits, information quality and security safeguards. The data controller, and anyone processing on its behalf, must notify the Commission and data subjects of unauthorised access or acquisition as soon as reasonably possible after discovery, unless the police, the National Security Service or the Commission ask for notice to data subjects to be delayed so as not to impede an investigation. It prohibits in principle the processing of sensitive information, governs rights of access and correction, unsolicited electronic marketing, automated decisions and transfers abroad, and provides for complaints, investigations and enforcement notices. Offences carry fines of up to M50,000 or imprisonment of up to five years.

items.summary: The law brings the main computer offences into Paraguay's Criminal Code. It punishes unauthorised access to data protected by security measures and the interception of data, with up to three and two years in prison, and the preparation of these offences by distributing passwords, access codes or programs designed to commit them. It adds unauthorised access to computer systems, including by exceeding an authorisation, and rewrites the offences of computer sabotage and computer fraud, punishable by up to five years. It introduces the forgery of debit and credit cards and other electronic payment instruments and updates the offence of child pornography.

items.summary: It is Costa Rica's general personal data protection law and protects the right to informational self-determination. It establishes the Agency for the Protection of Inhabitants' Data (PRODHAB), a body of the Ministry of Justice and Peace with instrumental legal personality, with which databases intended for distribution, dissemination or sale must be registered, subject to an annual fee. items.summary: The act sets general privacy principles for the handling of personal information and governs in separate parts data protection by public bodies and the private sector, transfers abroad, data matching and complaints. items.title: Personal Information Protection Act
items.officialTitle: 개인정보 보호법
items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · governance
items.summary: It is Korea's general personal data protection law, covering the public and private sectors and supervised by the Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC). It sets the legal bases for processing and rules on sensitive data, transfers abroad and the domestic representative of foreign controllers, and requires security measures, a chief privacy officer and notification of data leaks without delay to the people affected and to the PIPC or the designated body. Violations, including leaks caused by inadequate security measures, carry surcharges of up to 3% of total turnover. The amendment in force since 11 September 2026 raises the maximum to 10% for repeat violations within three years committed intentionally or with gross negligence, for violations affecting at least 10 million people and for leaks after a corrective order was ignored; it extends notification to cases of possible leaks, makes top management ultimately accountable and allows damages of up to five times the loss.

items.title: Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96)
items.officialTitle: The Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 96)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · cybercrime · critical infrastructure · financial sector
items.summary: The Act protects the security of information systems and electronic transactions and criminalises computer misuse. It punishes unauthorised access and interception, interference with data, devices for overcoming security measures, denial-of-service attacks, unauthorised modification, unauthorised use and obstruction of computer services, disclosure of access codes and electronic fraud, with life imprisonment where protected computers are involved, namely those linked to security and defence, communications, banking, public utilities or emergency services. It also creates content offences such as child pornography, cyber harassment and stalking, hate speech, unsolicited or malicious information and misuse of social media under a false identity. It governs data preservation and production orders, search and seizure and the admissibility of electronic evidence, and applies to acts committed outside Uganda.

items.title: Cyber Kill Chain: Intelligence-Driven Computer Network Defense Informed by Analysis of Adversary Campaigns and Intrusion Kill Chains
items.officialTitle: Cyber Kill Chain
items.topic: Cybersecurity standard · incident response · cyber defence
items.summary: The Cyber Kill Chain is Lockheed Martin’s model that breaks a targeted computer intrusion down into seven phases the attacker must go through in order: 1) reconnaissance (choosing the target and gathering information, such as email addresses); 2) weaponisation (coupling a remote access tool and an exploit into a file to send, such as a PDF or an Office document); 3) delivery (sending it to the target, usually by email, website or USB stick); 4) exploitation (the code is triggered through a vulnerability or through the user); 5) installation (a backdoor that keeps the attacker inside the system); 6) command and control (the channel through which the attacker steers the compromised system); 7) actions on objectives (theft, alteration or destruction of data, or moving on to other systems). The idea is that breaking a single phase stops the attack: for each phase the model offers a matrix of defensive actions (detect, deny, disrupt, degrade, deceive, destroy) and encourages the use of indicators gathered in past intrusions to recognise and anticipate campaigns by the same adversary. It is used in incident analysis, in threat intelligence and to check whether defences cover every phase.

items.title: Data Protection Act 2011
items.officialTitle: Data Protection Act (Act 11 of 2011)
items.summary: It is Saint Lucia's general personal data protection law. It establishes the Data Protection Commissioner, sets data protection principles and controllers' obligations (collection, consent, processing of sensitive, health and criminal data, accuracy, security, destruction, prohibition of unlawful disclosure, transfers abroad), provides for registration of controllers and recognises rights of access and rectification. Since 31 January 2023 only Part I, the controllers' obligations in sections 32 to 43, Part VI on exemptions and part of Schedule 2 are in force; the provisions on the Commissioner, registration and data subjects' rights await a ministerial order. Controllers must take appropriate security measures; the Act does not require breach notification. Unlawful disclosure and selling unlawfully obtained data are punishable by fines of up to 25,000 dollars or six months' imprisonment.

items.officialTitle: Computer Misuse Act (Act No. 12 of 2011)
items.summary: Saint Lucia's cybercrime law, which aims to protect the integrity of computer systems and the confidentiality, integrity and availability of data, prevent their misuse and make it easier to gather and use electronic evidence. It criminalises unauthorised access to data and systems, interception, unauthorised modification, damaging or blocking systems, disclosing passwords, possessing devices and data intended for offences, electronic fraud, indecent images of children and threatening or obscene communications. Heavier penalties, up to 100,000 Eastern Caribbean dollars or three years in prison, apply when the attack targets systems linked to security and defence, communications, banking and financial services, public utilities, transport or emergency services. The law also sets out investigative powers granted by a judge: expedited preservation and production orders, search and seizure of systems, and collection of traffic data with the help of service providers.

items.title: PDPA 2010 (Act 709) – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Akta Perlindungan Data Peribadi 2010 (Akta 709)
items.summary: It is Malaysia's general law on personal data processed in commercial transactions; it does not apply to the Federal or State Governments. It sets seven principles (general, notice and choice, disclosure, security, retention, data integrity and access), requires certain classes of data users to register and entrusts supervision to the Personal Data Protection Commissioner. Under the 2024 amendments by Act A1727, data processors are directly bound by the security principle, controllers must appoint a data protection officer and data subjects gain a right to data portability. A controller with reason to believe that a personal data breach has occurred must notify the Commissioner as soon as practicable and, where it is likely to cause significant harm, inform the data subjects without unnecessary delay. Breaching the principles is an offence punishable by a fine of up to one million ringgit and up to three years' imprisonment.

items.title: PDPA – Personal data protection (Taiwan)
items.officialTitle: 個人資料保護法 (Personal Data Protection Act)
items.summary: It is Taiwan's general law on the collection, processing and use of personal data by government agencies and private (non-government) bodies. It sets the legal bases for processing, notice to data subjects, rules on sensitive data (medical, genetic, criminal records and the like) and the rights of access, correction, deletion and objection, and allows cross-border transfers to be restricted. When data are stolen, altered, damaged, lost or leaked, the agency must notify the data subjects; the law sets no deadline in hours, leaving the details to rules of the competent authority. Violations by private bodies are punished with orders to rectify and fines repeated until compliance, alongside civil and criminal liability. The 2023 and 2025 amendments establish the Personal Data Protection Commission (PDPC) as an independent authority and strengthen supervision, breach reporting and penalties.

items.title: Law 998-IIIQ/2010 on Personal Data
items.officialTitle: "Fərdi məlumatlar haqqında" Azərbaycan Respublikasının Qanunu
items.summary: It is Azerbaijan's general law on personal data: it governs the collection, processing and protection of personal data by state and local bodies and by natural and legal persons, the personal data section of the national information space and cross-border data transfers. Data are classified as confidential or open; unless the law makes processing mandatory, the data subject's written consent is required (also in electronic form with an enhanced electronic signature), and stricter rules apply to special categories (racial or national origin, family life, religious beliefs, health, criminal convictions) and to biometric data. Data subjects have the right to be informed, to access their data, to request its correction or destruction and to object to processing; owners and operators of information systems must take technical and organisational security measures and answer requests within 7 working days. Personal data information systems must be registered with the relevant executive authority, which keeps the state register, checks compliance and can require violations to be remedied. Transfers abroad are prohibited if they threaten national security or if the destination country does not ensure a level of protection equal to Azerbaijan's, unless the data subject consents or the transfer is needed to protect their life and health; the Law does not provide for notification of data breaches.

It provides for the criminal liability of legal persons and governs expedited preservation and disclosure of data, production orders, search and seizure of data and email, interception and undercover operations. The Polícia Judiciária runs the 24/7 point of contact for international cooperation. Since 2025, access and interception carried out solely to identify and report vulnerabilities are not punishable under certain conditions.

items.title: Czech Criminal Code – Computer crime
items.officialTitle: Zákon č. 40/2009 Sb., trestní zákoník – ustanovení o počítačové kriminalitě
items.summary: The Czech Criminal Code criminalises access to a computer system by circumventing security measures and interference with a computer system or data carrier (section 230), covering unlawful use, deletion, damage, forgery and input of data and any other interference with software or hardware, with an aggravated penalty where the offence targets a system whose disruption would seriously affect the functioning of the State, health, security, the economy or the population's basic needs. It also criminalises producing and possessing devices, programs and passwords to commit these offences (section 231) and breach of the secrecy of transmitted messages, including messages in electronic communications networks and non-public transmissions of computer data (section 182). Other provisions cover child pornography, including accessing it through information technology (section 192), solicitation of children (section 193b), misuse of another person's identity to produce and distribute pornography (section 191a), stalking including by electronic communications (section 354), unlawful processing of personal data (section 180) and incitement to hatred (section 356).

items.summary: The Law, known as UU ITE, governs electronic information and documents, electronic signatures and certificates, electronic systems and electronic transactions in Indonesia, and is also the main criminal statute on computer crime. It prohibits and punishes the distribution of content that violates decency, relates to gambling, is defamatory or extortionate, false news harming consumers, incitement to hatred, threats, illegal access, interception, alteration and destruction of data and systems, tools for committing these offences and manipulation of electronic documents, with heavier penalties for government and strategic systems and liability for corporations. The Law was amended by Law No. 19 of 2016 and Law No. 1 of 2024, which reworded the offences of defamation, extortion and threats, strengthened the Government's power to block access to unlawful content and order content moderation, and placed child-protection duties on electronic system operators, backed by administrative sanctions.

On procedure, the investigating judge may order the expedited preservation of data for up to two years, search and seize computer systems including those connected to the initial one, and collect or intercept data in real time with the assistance of service providers; electronic writing is admitted as evidence and the Personal Data Protection Commission is informed of prosecutions for offences relating to personal data.

items.title: Federal Law 152-FZ on Personal Data
items.officialTitle: Федеральный закон от 27.07.2006 № 152-ФЗ «О персональных данных»
items.summary: It is Russia's general law on personal data. It governs the principles and conditions of processing, data subject consent, special categories of data and biometric data, data subjects' rights and the obligations of operators, who must take security measures and, with some exceptions, notify their processing to the federal supervisory authority (Roskomnadzor). Since 2022 it has also applied to foreign entities processing data of Russian citizens under a contract or with their consent, and cross-border transfers require prior notification to the authority. Since 1 July 2025 the recording, storage and other operations on collected data of Russian citizens may not be carried out using databases located abroad, except in a few cases. When an operator discovers an unlawful or accidental transfer of data that infringes data subjects' rights, it must inform the authority within 24 hours and report the results of its internal investigation within 72 hours.

items.title: Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 124B)
items.officialTitle: Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 124B)
items.summary: The Act protects computer systems and the information they contain against unauthorised access and against abuse by persons authorised to have access. It punishes illegal access, interference with data and computer systems, illegal interception, illegal devices, access with intent to commit further offences, unauthorised disclosure of access codes, offences involving restricted computer systems, child pornography and malicious communications. It also sets investigative powers: search and seizure of data, duties to assist the police, production and disclosure orders, preservation of data for criminal proceedings and compensation for victims. It applies to acts done in Barbados, on ships or aircraft registered in Barbados, or abroad by Barbadian nationals where the conduct is also an offence where it was committed.

items.regulator: Chambre des députés de la République tunisienne
items.title: Organic Law 2004-63 – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Loi organique n° 2004-63 du 27 juillet 2004, portant sur la protection des données à caractère personnel
items.summary: It is Tunisia's general personal data protection law, which recognises data protection as a fundamental right, and applies to automated and non-automated processing by natural and legal persons; personal or household use is excluded. All processing must be declared in advance to the National Authority for the Protection of Personal Data (INPDP), whose silence for one month counts as acceptance; its authorisation is required instead for sensitive data (racial or genetic origin, religious beliefs, political, philosophical or trade union opinions), video surveillance, disclosure to third parties without consent and every transfer abroad, which is banned where it may harm public security or the country's vital interests. Consent must be express and written; for children the guardian's consent and the family judge's authorisation are needed. Controllers and their staff must be Tunisian nationals, resident in Tunisia and without a criminal record. The law sets security obligations, the rights of access, rectification and objection and special rules for public authorities, health, research and video surveillance. The INPDP grants authorisations, carries out inspections and may ban processing. There is no obligation to notify data breaches. Penalties are criminal, up to five years' imprisonment and a fine of 50,000 dinars for prohibited transfers abroad.

items.title: HSPD-7 – Critical infrastructure protection
items.officialTitle: Homeland Security Presidential Directive 7: Critical Infrastructure Identification, Prioritization, and Protection
items.summary: Presidential directive of 17 December 2003 establishing the national policy for federal departments and agencies to identify and prioritise United States critical infrastructure and key resources and to protect them from terrorist attacks. It makes the Secretary of Homeland Security responsible for coordinating the overall national effort, as the principal federal official to lead, integrate and coordinate implementation, and requires a National Plan for Critical Infrastructure and Key Resources Protection within one year. It lists the sectors, including information technology, telecommunications, chemicals, transportation systems, emergency services and postal and shipping, and assigns sector responsibilities to the relevant agencies: Agriculture, Health and Human Services, the Environmental Protection Agency for drinking water, Energy, the Treasury for banking and finance, the Interior for national monuments and icons, and Defense for the defense industrial base. It supersedes Presidential Decision Directive/NSC-63 of 1998.

items.summary: Italy's Personal Data Protection Code, rewritten by Legislative Decree 101/2018 to bring it into line with the GDPR and now confined to the matters the Regulation leaves to Member States. It governs the legal bases for public-interest processing and for special categories of data, sets the age of children's consent to information society services at 14 and contains sector rules (health, employment, research, journalism, electronic communications, marketing). It regulates the organisation, powers and procedures of the supervisory authority, the Garante per la protezione dei dati personali, including complaints and administrative sanctions. It establishes offences such as unlawful processing of data (six months to eighteen months' imprisonment) and unlawful large-scale disclosure of data (one to six years). Breach notification follows Article 33 GDPR (to the Garante within 72 hours).

items.title: APPI – Protection of personal information
items.officialTitle: 個人情報の保護に関する法律（平成十五年法律第五十七号）
items.summary: Japan's law on the protection of personal information, substantially reformed in 2015, 2020 and 2021, when it unified the rules for the private sector, national administrative organs, incorporated administrative agencies and local governments. It imposes on businesses handling personal information duties concerning purposes of use, acquisition, security control measures, supervision of employees and trustees, provision to third parties and transfers abroad, with rules on pseudonymised and anonymised information and rights of disclosure, correction and cessation of use. It is overseen by the Personal Information Protection Commission (PPC), an independent authority with powers of inspection, recommendation and order. Leaks and other incidents likely to harm individual rights and interests must be reported to the PPC and notified to the persons concerned within the time limits set by the Commission's rules. Violating orders and unlawfully providing personal information databases are offences, punishable for corporations by fines of up to 100 million yen.

items.regulator: U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (HHS)
items.title: HIPAA Security Rule
items.officialTitle: HIPAA Security Rule: Health Insurance Reform; Security Standards (45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, Subparts A and C)
items.summary: The Security Rule implements the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) of 1996 and sets the US national standards for protecting electronic protected health information (ePHI). It applies to healthcare providers, health plans and clearinghouses and, since 2013, to the vendors that handle health data on their behalf (business associates). It requires risk analysis and risk management and administrative, physical and technical safeguards: access control, audit controls, data integrity, authentication and transmission security. Some safeguards are required, others must be adopted where reasonable and appropriate for the entity. It is enforced by the Office for Civil Rights of the Department of Health and Human Services.

items.title: Computer Crimes Act (Act 14 of 2003, CAP. 10.06)
items.officialTitle: Computer Crimes Act (Act 14 of 2003, CAP. 10.06)
items.summary: The Act combats computer crime and governs the collection and use of electronic evidence. It punishes illegal access, interference with data and systems, illegal interception and illegal devices, with penalties of up to 20 years' imprisonment for access to protected computers, such as those used for security, law enforcement, banking, public utilities and transport. It gives the police powers of search and seizure, orders for production and disclosure of traffic data, data preservation and interception of electronic communications and traffic data.

items.regulator: Asamblea Nacional de la República Bolivariana de Venezuela
items.title: Special Law on Cybercrimes
items.officialTitle: Ley Especial contra los Delitos Informáticos
items.summary: Venezuela's cybercrime law, aimed at the comprehensive protection of systems that use information technology and at preventing and punishing offences committed against such systems or by means of them. It defines technical terms and punishes, with prison terms of up to ten years and fines in tax units, five groups of offences: against systems (unlawful access, sabotage and damage, possessing or supplying sabotage tools, computer espionage, document forgery), against property (theft, fraud, fraudulent use of cards and payment instruments), against the privacy of data and communications, against children (distribution of pornographic material) and against the economic order (infringement of intellectual property, misleading offers). Penalties increase when the acts affect systems protected by security measures, used for public functions or holding personal or financial data. The law provides for the liability of legal persons, additional penalties, publication of the judgment, compensation for victims and application to acts committed abroad that have effects in Venezuela.

items.regulator: National Assembly of the Republic of Korea
items.title: Korea's Information and Communications Network Act
items.officialTitle: 정보통신망 이용촉진 및 정보보호 등에 관한 법률
items.topic: Cybersecurity · incident reporting · incident response · telecommunications · certification · governance
items.summary: It is Korea's main law on the security of information and communications networks and services in the private sector. It requires service providers to take protective measures and appoint a chief information security officer (CISO), who since 2026 must be an executive; major operators and data centres must obtain information security management system (ISMS) certification. Under the amendment promulgated on 31 March 2026 and in force since 1 October 2026, providers must report intrusions to the Ministry of Science and ICT or KISA within 24 hours of becoming aware of them and notify affected users of the most serious incidents without delay. The ministry can order cause analysis and corrective measures, supported by an incident investigation review committee, and impose surcharges of up to 3% of turnover when two or more incidents caused by intent or gross negligence occur within five years. The Act also covers spam, illegal content and the protection of minors online.
