items.title: Law 133/V/2001 – Personal data protection
items.officialTitle: Lei n.º 133/V/2001, de 22 de janeiro – Regime jurídico geral de proteção de dados pessoais das pessoas singulares
items.topic: Cybersecurity · data protection · incident reporting · governance
items.summary: It is Cabo Verde's general law on the protection of personal data of natural persons, modelled on Portuguese Law 67/98 and Directive 95/46/EC and amended in 2013 and 2021. It governs the principles and lawful grounds for processing, special categories of data (including biometric data and sexual orientation), data subjects' rights, notification and prior checking of processing by the Comissão Nacional de Proteção de Dados (CNPD) and transfers abroad. The 2021 reform brought it closer to the GDPR: it extends its scope to controllers established abroad that process data of persons in Cabo Verde and introduces pseudonymisation and profiling, data protection by design and impact assessments. Controllers must notify personal data breaches to the CNPD within 72 hours of becoming aware of them, unless they pose no risk, and inform data subjects where the risk is high. Infringements are punished with administrative fines and ancillary sanctions imposed by the CNPD.

items.title: Computer Misuse Act 2000
items.officialTitle: Computer Misuse Act, 2000, Chap. 11:17 (Act No. 86 of 2000)
items.summary: It is Trinidad and Tobago's computer crime law. It punishes unauthorised access to programs or data, access with intent to commit or facilitate other offences, unauthorised modification of programs or data, unauthorised use or interception of computer services, obstruction of the use of a computer, unlawful disclosure of passwords and access codes, unauthorised receiving or giving of programs or data, and conduct that causes a computer to cease to function. The basic offences carry a fine of 15,000 dollars and two years' imprisonment (30,000 dollars and four years for repeat offences), with additional penalties where damage is caused. Where the offence involves a protected computer, that is, one used for the security, defence or international relations of the State, for confidential law-enforcement sources, for communications infrastructure, banking and financial services, public utilities, public transportation or public key infrastructure, or for public safety and health, the penalty rises to 150,000 dollars and ten years. The Act also applies to acts committed abroad where the accused, the computer or the damage is in the country; courts may order compensation, and the police, under a magistrate's warrant, may search, access computers, including encrypted data, and seize evidence.

items.regulator: Congreso de la Nación Argentina (National Congress)
items.title: Law No. 25.326 on Personal Data Protection
items.officialTitle: Ley 25.326 de Protección de los Datos Personales
items.summary: Argentina's personal data protection law (also known as the habeas data law), implementing Article 43 of the Constitution. It applies to public files, registers and databases and to private ones intended to provide reports, and lays down the principles of lawfulness, data quality, informed consent, security and confidentiality, with special rules for sensitive data and credit-reporting services. It grants rights of information, access, rectification, updating and erasure and the habeas data court action, and prohibits transfers to countries without an adequate level of protection. The control body, today the Agency for Access to Public Information (AAIP), may issue warnings, suspensions, fines of 1,000 to 100,000 pesos (amounts set in the original text) and order databases closed. The law contains no personal data breach notification duty.

items.officialTitle: The Information Technology Act, 2000 (Act No. 21 of 2000)
items.topic: Cybersecurity · cybercrime · incident response · incident reporting · critical infrastructure · digital identity

items.title: PIPEDA – Personal information protection
items.officialTitle: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (S.C. 2000, c. 5)
items.summary: Canada's federal law on the protection of personal information in the private sector. It applies to organisations that collect, use or disclose personal information in the course of commercial activities, except in provinces with legislation recognised as substantially similar, and incorporates the ten principles of the CSA Model Code (accountability, purposes, consent, limiting, accuracy, safeguards, openness, access and challenging compliance). It is overseen by the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, who investigates complaints, conducts audits and may apply to the Federal Court. Since 2018 organisations must report to the Commissioner, and notify affected individuals of, breaches of security safeguards creating a real risk of significant harm, as soon as feasible, and keep records of all breaches. Certain contraventions, including knowingly failing to report a breach, are offences punishable by fines of up to 100,000 Canadian dollars.

items.title: Computer Misuse Act (Cap. 194)
items.officialTitle: Computer Misuse Act (Chapter 194)
items.summary: The Act secures computer material against unauthorised access or modification. It punishes unauthorised access to computer material, access with intent to commit or facilitate other offences, unauthorised modification of programs and data, unauthorised use or interception of computer services, unauthorised obstruction of the use of a computer and unauthorised disclosure of access codes, including attempts and abetment. items.summary: Chapter XX of the Latvian Criminal Law (offences against general safety and public order) criminalises unauthorised access to an automated data processing system (Section 241), alteration, damage, destruction or concealment of information and interference with the operation of the system (Section 243), with aggravated penalties where the offences target systems processing information connected with the political, economic, military, social or other security of the State, and making, distributing or possessing devices, programs, passwords and access codes to commit offences (Section 244). Other provisions criminalise violation of the secrecy of correspondence and interception of non-public data transmissions in electronic communications networks (Section 144), computer fraud (Section 177.1), solicitation of children through information technology (Section 162.1), child pornography (Section 166), stalking (Section 132.1) and incitement to national, ethnic, racial or religious hatred, aggravated where committed through an automated data processing system (Section 78).

items.title: Spanish Criminal Code – Computer crime
items.officialTitle: Ley Orgánica 10/1995, de 23 de noviembre, del Código Penal – delitos informáticos
items.summary: The Spanish Criminal Code places computer crimes among the offences against privacy and against property. It criminalises unauthorised access to an information system by breaching security measures and interception of non-public data transmissions (Art. 197 bis), producing or supplying programs and passwords to commit these offences (Art. 197 ter), damage to data, programs and electronic documents (Art. 264), aggravated where it affects essential public services or the computer system of a critical infrastructure, serious hindering of the functioning of a computer system (Art. 264 bis) and the tools for committing them (Art. 264 ter); legal persons are criminally liable for them (Arts. 197 quinquies and 264 quater). Computer fraud is punished as fraud (Art. 249). Other provisions cover the discovery and disclosure of secrets and personal data (Art. 197), online grooming of minors (Art. 183), child pornography (Art. 189), stalking and fake social media profiles (Art. 172 ter) and incitement to hatred (Art. 510); computer crimes committed for terrorist purposes are terrorist offences (Art. 573).

items.topic: Cybersecurity · cybercrime · digital identity · data protection
items.summary: The Act secures computer material against unauthorised access or modification and is Singapore's main computer crime statute. items.title: Privacy Act 1988
items.officialTitle: Privacy Act 1988
items.summary: Australia's federal law on the protection of personal information, amended many times, most recently by the Privacy and Other Legislation Amendment Act 2024. It subjects federal agencies and private organisations to the 13 Australian Privacy Principles on collection, use, disclosure, quality, security, access, correction and cross-border disclosure of information, with specific rules for credit reporting and APP codes. The Notifiable Data Breaches scheme (Part IIIC) requires entities to notify the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) and affected individuals of breaches likely to result in serious harm: the assessment must be completed within 30 days and notification made as soon as practicable. Serious interferences with privacy carry civil penalties of up to the greater of AUD 50 million, three times the benefit obtained or 30% of adjusted turnover. The 2024 amendments also created a statutory tort for serious invasions of privacy and transparency duties for automated decisions.

items.title: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. § 1030)
items.officialTitle: Computer Fraud and Abuse Act (18 U.S.C. § 1030, Fraud and related activity in connection with computers)
items.summary: Section 1030 of Title 18 of the United States Code is the main federal criminal provision against computer crime. It punishes anyone who accesses a computer without authorization or exceeds authorized access to obtain classified defence information, financial records, information from federal agencies or information from any "protected computer", which in practice covers any computer used in interstate or foreign commerce. Computer fraud, knowingly transmitting a program or command that intentionally damages a protected computer, trafficking in passwords and extortion through threats to damage systems or data are also offences. Penalties reach ten years' imprisonment for first offences and twenty years, or life imprisonment, in the most serious cases. Anyone who suffers damage or loss may also bring a civil action within two years of the act or of the discovery of the damage.

items.title: French Data Protection Act (Law 78-17)
items.officialTitle: Loi n° 78-17 du 6 janvier 1978 relative à l'informatique, aux fichiers et aux libertés
items.summary: France's personal data protection law, one of the first in Europe, rewritten by Ordinance No. 2018-1125 to supplement the GDPR and transpose Directive (EU) 2016/680. It governs the Commission nationale de l'informatique et des libertés (CNIL), an independent administrative authority, its supervisory powers and the sanctioning procedure before its restricted committee, including fines within the limits of Article 83 GDPR. It specifies national rules on sensitive data, criminal-offence data, health research and the national registration number, and sets the age of children's consent to information society services at 15. Separate titles govern police and criminal-justice processing, processing concerning State security and defence, data altruism and the supervision of online platforms. For personal data breaches Articles 33 and 34 GDPR apply (notification to the CNIL within 72 hours), including to processing in criminal matters.

items.title: Privacy Act of 1974
items.officialTitle: Privacy Act of 1974
items.summary: The Privacy Act is the US federal law that protects personal records held by federal agencies. It sets a code of fair information practices: agencies must publish notice of their systems of records in the Federal Register, collect only relevant information and keep it accurate and up to date, and put in place administrative, technical and physical safeguards to protect it. Records may not be disclosed without the individual's written consent, except under twelve statutory exceptions, and every person can access their records and ask for them to be corrected, including in court. The law does not apply to private companies or to the states: the United States has no general federal data protection law, but sector laws (health, finance, children) and state laws such as California's CCPA.

items.title: Brottsbalken – Computer crime

items.summary: The Swedish Criminal Code criminalises data breach (dataintrång, chapter 4, section 9 c), which in a single provision covers unauthorised access to data intended for automated processing, its alteration, deletion or blocking and serious disruption of its use, with up to eight years' imprisonment in serious cases. It also criminalises breach of postal or telecommunication secrecy (chapter 4, section 8), computer fraud, i.e. unlawfully influencing the result of automated information processing (chapter 9, section 1, second paragraph), forgery of electronic documents (chapter 14, section 1), unlawful use of another person's identity (chapter 4, section 6 b) and dissemination of images or information about a person's sex life, health or naked body (chapter 4, section 6 c). Other provisions cover contact with a child for sexual purposes (chapter 6, section 10 a), child sexual abuse material (chapter 16, section 10 a) and agitation against a population group (chapter 16, section 8).

items.title: Straffeloven – Computer crime

items.title: StGB – Computer crime provisions

items.summary: The German Criminal Code contains the main computer crime provisions. Other provisions cover child sexual abuse material, grooming of children through content, intimate image recording, stalking including by computer means and incitement to hatred.

This record describes the official applicability status and does not claim the EU AI Act is already part of Liechtenstein’s domestic law. Check the government’s EEA monitoring list for current incorporation status.

items.title: Railway applications – Cybersecurity
items.summary: This is the future international cybersecurity standard for the whole railway system, developed by IEC Technical Committee 9 from the European specification CLC/TS 50701 and the IEC 62443 series. It covers signalling, rolling stock, fixed installations and communications, with a cyber risk management process integrated into the railway system lifecycle and functional safety. It will be adopted in parallel as the European standard EN IEC 63452 and will take over from the CENELEC technical specification.
